articles.title: Trump's $50B air traffic control overhaul faces GOP pushback after nationwide ground stop
articles.summary: Senate Republicans want receipts on the $12.5 billion already sent for air traffic control as the Trump administration seeks $50 billion more.
articles.body: The Trump administration is pressing Congress for tens of billions in emergency funding to upgrade the nation’s air traffic control systems, but even Senate Republicans are reluctant to pay the bill. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and President Donald Trump called on lawmakers to shell out $50 billion in funding after a ground stop on Friday caused thousands of flight cancellations and blamed Congress for not doling out money previously to upgrade aging air traffic control communications infrastructure. But Congress did send $12.5 billion to the Department of Transportation as part of the "big, beautiful bill" last year meant to upgrade the archaic systems, and Republicans want receipts on what happened to the money. FAA SAYS AIR TRAVEL SHOULD BE BACK TO NORMAL SUNDAY AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP "Only about four [billion] has been spent," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said. "There was about eight billion of that still sitting around." Duffy is slated to meet with Senate Republicans behind closed doors on Tuesday where lawmakers expect a full breakdown of what happened and where the money has gone and why, suddenly, the administration is seeking an additional $20 billion. "I haven't seen how they're gonna use it. I mean, in my business, you know, I spent a lot of money, and I built companies," Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital. "And I understood what I was going to spend it on before I ever did anything. I'd have a budget and what the timeline is, who's gonna do it, all that stuff." FORMER TOP FAA OFFICIAL WARNS OF 48-HOUR RECOVERY AFTER AGING TECH 'OVERWHELMED' AHEAD OF GROUND STOP Data from the Department of Transportation (DOT) obtained by Fox News Digital showed that roughly $3.7 billion had been spent on a variety of projects, while the remainder is tied to contracts, unspent or planned for near-term upgrades, like facility consolidation. Thune declined to say whether he had confidence in Duffy’s handling of the situation and noted that the administration had already made a separate ask for $30 billion, a chunk of which was meant to continue upgrades to air traffic control. "I mean, there's some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is," Thune said. "But I think we have attempted to do everything we can to ensure that the concerns they have about modernization are being met." Duffy’s explanation of the ground stop was attributed to replacing copper wiring in communications equipment with fiber-optic cable. About $4.8 billion of the initial funding pot was for copper wire replacement, of which about $2.3 billion has been spent, which translates to roughly 70% completion of the telecommunications replacement program, according to the DOT. 4 CRITICAL TRAVEL ISSUES FOR THOSE DELAYED AND DISRUPTED BY FAA NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP A DOT spokesperson told Fox News Digital that the "Department has made clear for the last two years — separate funding is needed" for other work because DOT "does not have the legal flexibility to move funds from one workstream to another." Still, lawmakers have questions. "He needs to talk to me like I'm a reasonably intelligent 10th grader," Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said. "The American people are not experts on telecommunications … nor am I." Kennedy, who is a member of the Transportation, Housing and Urban Development Appropriations Subcommittee, which controls the DOT's purse strings, said he was more than "willing to appropriate money to fix this," but needed to understand the problem first. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I mean, we had an outage today, some problems with a number of our banks," Kennedy said. "There have been some problems in Europe with the Internet controlling temperatures of grocery stores. I mean, this is happening a lot. I'm not saying there's a connection, but if there is, they need to tell us." Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., told Fox News Digital that the initial $12.5 billion was "a starting point — it wasn’t everything." "We've seen nothing yet of what's the rest of the request," Lankford said. "So that does seem like, ‘Hey, grab a number out of the air. It needs to be big.’" Lankford added that Duffy needed to give a "postmortem" on what happened, and that whatever the administration is asking for in upgrades needs to be "shovel-ready." "This is a zero fail operation," he said. "He's keenly aware of that."

articles.title: Hundreds protest against ex-border patrol chief Greg Bovino at Rutgers University talk
articles.summary: New Jersey university’s Republicans club invited Bovino, who oversaw Trump’s ICE surges, to speak on campus
articles.body:
Hundreds protested outside a Rutgers University campus building on Monday night, jeering the former border patrol commander Greg Bovino, who was inside addressing a crowd of about 25 people.

The university's Republicans club had invited Bovino to speak, calling him the "Great Commander" and the "GOAT" in social posts promoting the event at the New Brunswick, New Jersey, campus. During the two-hour talk, the room never quite filled up, occupied mostly by journalists, club members and other students criticizing the former border patrol chief.

"Show of hands, can we remove 100 million illegal aliens by 2028? Do you think we can?" Bovino asked the crowd. Two or three hands went into the air. "Well, I'm telling you what, my hand's raised! American exceptionalism! We can do it before then!"

Bovino was the face of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, overseeing massive Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) surges in Chicago, Minneapolis and other US cities. Scrutiny and public outrage over agents' brutal handling of immigrant arrests, pulling children off the streets and taking people from cars, only intensified after agents killed the Minneapolis residents Alex Pretti and Renee Good in January. Bovino, who argued Pretti was a "suspect" rather than a victim, was taken out of the field by the end of the month and retired in March, reportedly while under internal investigation .

A few minutes into his talk on Monday, about a dozen protesters drowned out his remarks. "What's so crazy is that you all allowed a Nazi to be here," one protester shouted over him, standing from her seat.

"Your fascist death cult is failing!" yelled another. Several police officers gathered in front of a grinning Bovino on stage, who seemed to be relishing the attention.

Helping lead the disruption was immigration advocate Gabriela Soto, whose husband, Martín, helped lead hunger strikes over conditions and deaths at the Delaney Hall immigration detention facility in New Jersey earlier this year. When Martín was transferred to another facility in May , intense protests ensued for weeks .

Gabriela was pregnant when Martín was taken into ICE custody; while he was held in solitary confinement, she miscarried.

"You're taking children!" she screamed, standing on a chair at the Rutgers event. "It's not OK!"

Bovino eventually left the stage for a few minutes, while police ordered protesters to either stop the disruption or disperse; they largely complied. He then returned to give his talk, in which he repeatedly mentioned a small Michigan city that banned LGBTQ+ pride flags in 2023, made a seemingly homophobic pun out of Pete Buttigieg's last name and ridiculed New Jersey's governor, Mikie Sherrill, who earlier on Monday issued a statement condemning the event without ordering its cancellation.

Even among the smaller crowd, multiple people expressed their disagreement with Bovino during a question-and-answer session. When retired teacher Alan Cummings asked about his goal of 100m deportations, even though the estimated number of undocumented immigrants in the US is a fraction of that, he argued Cummings wasn't proud to be American.

After Rutgers's College Republicans announced the event last month, it was immediately met with backlash. The ICE Out of New Jersey coalition , comprising several advocacy organizations, and student organizers called on the university to cancel it. The students' petition garnered more than 2,000 signatures.

Dory Devlin, assistant vice-president of news and media relations at Rutgers, said the university was committed to freedom of expression, but that "providing space for a student-organized event does not constitute university endorsement of the speaker or the views expressed".

"We are all about free speech," said Brea Yumiguano, a Rutgers senior and student organizer with Climate Revolution Action Network. "The issue comes when it's Greg Bovino, someone who has been violent in the past, who has eroded our constitutional rights, who's pepper-sprayed protesters in Minneapolis – that's not what we want in New Brunswick."

Yumiguano and other students at the protest talked about the lack of safety facing immigrant students, students with immigrant family members and international students who fear being targeted by ICE. Earlier that Monday, it was reported that US international student enrollment had dropped for the second consecutive year amid the Trump administration's ICE campaign.

A Rutgers sophomore named Ninnie broke down in tears while telling the crowd she did not feel safe bringing her family to campus, describing reports of ICE agents targeting local public transportation. "There are plenty of us students here who are people of color who are afraid to have our family members come visit us at Rutgers," she told the crowd.

After more than an hour of chanting to drums and bagpipes, most of the protesters left. Eventually, those who remained at Bovino's talk trickled out through the security perimeter established by police. A "prosecute Bovino" sign was left by the exit door.

"This is an example of what New Jersey is about: New Jersey is an immigrants' rights state. We welcome immigrants," said Jorge Torres of the National Day Laborer Organizing Network, a member of the ICE Out coalition. Torres was among those who interrupted Bovino's speech. "We don't want no neo-Nazis in our state."

images.caption: Protesters disrupt former border patrol commander Greg Bovino's appearance at the Rutgers University campus in New Brunswick, New Jersey, on Monday. Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPA

articles.title: Let's be honest, no politician is coming to save you, so save yourself first
articles.summary: A Chicago pastor who spent 94 days on a motel roof after gang violence killed 16-year-old Carlton Archer says elections won't pay your rent.
articles.body: Two weeks ago, on Nov. 3, many of us Americans voted. We watched the election returns come in on cable and broadcast news that night. We were flooded with takes on the results from so-called media experts. And now our newly elected officials are waiting in the wings to take office in the new year. But for most of us, on the first of the month, the rent will still be due. I say this because our elected officials are not our saviors. I didn’t vote for either of Chicago’s last two mayors. Neither one of them did much for our community. Nor will the newly elected, despite all of their promises. Down here on the South Side of Chicago, I have mothers who let their mailboxes overflow because they’re afraid of seeing the bills they can’t pay. There are fathers looking for work. Too many of our young people have watched their friends get buried or locked up. And the rent, the light bill, the groceries and the car note do not care who won the election. I believe we give far too much credit to politicians. The best of our society often do not run for office, and those representing us are not the best of us. We cannot afford false idols any longer. In my community work, I tell people to forget about anyone coming to save their butt. The first one who is going to save you is you. You have to save yourself before anyone can help you. PASTOR COREY BROOKS: EL-SAYED'S PITCH TO BLACK VOTERS IS THE SAME OLD LIBERAL CONDESCENSION I learned that the hard way. I didn’t grow up here. I was born in Kenton, Tennessee, and raised in Muncie, Indiana. I thought I wanted to be a lawyer until I heard God calling me. I became a pastor, and I eventually came to Chicago, where I started my New Beginnings Church in 2000. I started this church for young people who had never been connected to a church. In those early years, I was told I had to be part of the political machine to get things done. I remember people trying to get me on the Jesse Jackson bandwagon, and I met with a lot of those people. However, I felt a profound disconnect between that world of politics, racial politics, and the Christian work I was doing on the ground with my congregation. The violence was out of control. The drug use was ungodly. The number of single-parent households was staggering. My issue with this Chicago political machine was that the solution was always political. These politicians held themselves out as the solutions. Their policies were the solutions. Yet things got worse. DIVINE PURPOSE HELPED BRING CHICAGO’S MOST-DANGEROUS BLOCK BACK TO LIFE Then, in 2011, I received the terrible news that Carlton Archer, a 16-year-old boy, had been shot. He was a member of our church until gang violence took his life. For some reason, his death shook me. I think it was because I knew that no politician was going to come and make his death mean something or prevent future tragedies like Carlton's. The only help was going to come from God, me and the people. I buried Carlton. I gave his eulogy. Then I felt a nudge on my shoulder, and I turned around, but there was no one there. I felt the nudge again, and I knew it was from God. I walked out the door and across the street to the Super Motel, which was a hellhole of murder, drugs and prostitution. I said to myself, "Carlton’s death must mean something. It must move us to action." I placed a ladder against the side of the motel and climbed to the roof in the middle of the winter, where I stayed for 94 days. We raised enough to purchase the motel and tear it down. Instantly, the neighborhood saw a drop in overall crime. I knew it was Carlton saving lives. COREY BROOKS: CHICAGO SCHOOLS ARE FAILING KIDS AT THE ONE SKILL THAT CAN CHANGE THEIR LIVES It wasn’t the political class that did this. They would have talked themselves to death and planned themselves to death. It was the nudge from above that did this. It was the people who supported us through the entire journey that did this. It was that spark that set me off on a 15-year journey to build a community center in place of that motel. I even went back on top of a roof built atop shipping containers for 345 days to raise millions. All because I wouldn’t let Carlton’s death go to waste. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Today, the Robert R. McCormick Leadership & Economic Opportunity Center stands impressively along King Drive. It is roughly 90,000 square feet of classrooms, trade training facilities, a gym, and a culinary school with restaurants opening onto the sidewalk. Within this space, people used to murder, fornicate and get high, and now, in this very same space, people are learning to wire a building, fix an engine and run a kitchen. If that is not a miracle, I don’t know what it is. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP I did all of this without government money. That is why I tell people to, yes, pay attention to elections and vote wisely. But I tell them to never put their fate in the hands of politicians. They work for us. Make them work for you. And throughout all of this, never lose sight of the most important American in your life: you. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM PASTOR COREY BROOKS

articles.title: ASRA NOMANI: Far-left US groups battle Trump plan to rival China's tech dominance
articles.summary: The "Shut Down Pax" campaign, backed by CodePink and groups tied to Neville Roy Singham, fights President Donald Trump's bid to cut U.S. reliance on China.
articles.body: As President Donald Trump attends the 49th ASEAN Summit in the Philippines, American communist and far-left organizations are mobilizing internationally against an American initiative designed to reduce reliance on China. According to a Fox News Digital investigation, a network of 120 mostly communist, socialist and far-left U.S. groups – many of them pro-China – are joining protests in Asia opposing the Trump administration's effort to build an artificial intelligence and semiconductor hub in the Philippines that would reduce U.S. dependence on China in the AI war. The target is the Pax Silica tech industrial hub in the Philippines, which Undersecretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg, a former senior adviser at Palantir Technologies, said last year would strengthen American control over AI infrastructure, semiconductor production and critical mineral supply chains. Two days ago, Helberg described Pax Silica as key to the world's "superintelligence revolution." The dispute centers partly on the proposed Clark Advanced Manufacturing Park, a roughly 4,000-acre development in New Clark City, Tarlac, in the Philippines, that would be a hub for the Pax Silica project. UPDATED – CHAOS INC.: COMMUNISTS, ANTIFA, AGITATORS IN THE RED-GREEN ALLIANCE A Fox News Digital investigation traced support for the protests to a transnational pro-China activist network stretching from Manila to New York, Washington, D.C., Los Angeles and Canada, including the Democratic Socialists of America East Bay, Calif., chapter and organizations with ties to American-born, Shanghai-based Marxist tech millionaire Neville Roy Singham. The protests also include indigenous groups in the Philippines that allege Pax Silica is being built on ancestral land. About eight of 10 of the organizations in the network of 120 are openly communist, socialist or "anti-imperialist." TRUMP TO SIGN TRADE DEAL AS HE KICKS OFF ASIA TRIP AHEAD OF NUCLEAR TALKS WITH XI AND PUTIN In addition, most of them are openly "anti-Zionist," opposed to the existence of a Jewish state of Israel, according to a Fox News Digital analysis of the groups in the network. CodePink, a pro-communist, pro-China nonprofit co-founded by Singham's wife, Jodie Evans, has used its media programming to criticize Pax Silica as a "military-industrial-surveillance complex." For Washington, experts say, the Pax Silica plan is about securing the technology and resources needed to compete with Beijing. For opponents, the protests are a way to curb American economic and military domination. The campaign also reveals how opposition to Trump's China strategy is being organized not only overseas, but through pro-China activist networks inside the United States. TRUMP LEAVES DOOR OPEN TO KIM JONG UN JOINING HIGH-STAKES TALKS WITH XI, PUTIN The U.S. network, organizing behind a campaign called "Shut Down Pax," includes familiar faces in the Singham network's protest circuit: BAYAN USA, a pro-communist Filipino American alliance helping lead the campaign; Anakbayan USA, a pro-communist youth organization; and the International League of Peoples' Struggle, or ILPS, founded with the help of Jose Maria Sison, the late founder of the Communist Party of the Philippines. The campaign has also reached the U.S. Congress. A letter, headlined "Shut Down Pax Silica in the Philippines" calls on lawmakers to halt the initiative pending review of environmental protections, labor rights and the treatment of Philippine communities. The activism intersects with other nonprofits in the network funded by Singham, including the People's Forum and BreakThrough News, that have promoted opposition to American foreign policy and challenged Washington's confrontation with Beijing. On Sept. 20, the U.S. chapter of the International League of Peoples' Struggle, the International Coalition for Human Rights in the Philippines-US and Bagong Alyansang Makabayan USA, or BAYAN USA, launched the "Shut Down Pax Silica Campaign Network" in Queens, New York, with organizers claiming about 500 participants in person and online. An article, published by Bulatlat, invoked a term popular in communist, "anti-imperialist" circles, claiming that a movement had begun in "the belly of the beast," with "resistance" to Pax Silica "rising." "We unite to confront and oppose the Trump/U.S.-led Pax Silica Initiative in its competition with China to dominate the AI/tech supply chain," the coalition declared in its organizing platform. FIRST ON FOX: ‘NO KINGS’ PROTEST NETWORK BEHIND FIGHT AGAINST AI DATA CENTERS AND FLOCK CAMERAS "We Filipinos in the U.S. must also take action," BAYAN USA declares on its campaign website, urging opposition to U.S. investments associated with Pax Silica. A month later, on Oct. 24, CodePink Radio published Episode 374, with host Marcy Winograd interviewing sociologist William Robinson about his new book, "Pax Silica: The New Ruling Class," examining the "rise of a new transnational capital complex" that combines big tech with global finance and the "military-industrial-surveillance complex" to "colonize the world unless we continue to protest, disrupt, divest and withhold our labor." The Black Alliance for Peace, which participated in CodePink's November "Taxpayer Uprising" campaign in Washington, D.C., last week, also promoted the anti-Pax Silica campaign's launch. Anakbayan USA, its local chapters and GABRIELA USA, a Filipino women's organization, appear among the American coalition's participants. Their Philippine counterparts are involved in the demonstrations surrounding Trump's visit. The coalition's published platform also identifies "Migrante USA," student organizations and other activist groups. The overlapping campaigns bring together Filipino American organizations, socialist activists and groups that have previously organized against U.S. military operations, Israel and American foreign policy. Singham, an American-born technology entrepreneur who sold his consultancy ThoughtWorks for an estimated $785 million in 2017, has financed an extensive network of U.S. nonprofits. A Fox News Digital investigation traced $278 million into six core American nonprofits, including CodePink, People's Forum, Tricontinental and BreakThrough BT Media Inc., which operates BreakThrough News. AMERICA RUNS ON DATA. IF WE DON’T BUILD THE INFRASTRUCTURE, CHINA WILL In July, the House Ways and Means Committee subpoenaed three organizations as lawmakers investigated the financial network and potential foreign influence. The organizations have challenged the investigation. One connection to the anti-Pax Silica campaign from the Singham network is "Nodutdol for Korean Community Development," an American group listed among the coalition's endorsers. Nodutdol member Winter Oh participated in the September launch in Queens. BreakThrough News has amplified the Philippine protests and criticism of Pax Silica, this summer promoting a BAYAN and Kilusang Mayo Uno demonstration with the slogan "The Philippines is not for sale!" As Trump was still in flight to Manila, BreakThrough news highlighted growing opposition to Pax Silica with a story headline, "ASEAN summit in Manila met with protests over Trump’s participation." Philippine officials have previously accused organizations such as Gabriela, Anakbayan, Karapatan and Kilusang Mayo Uno of acting as communist fronts. The groups have denied those allegations. CODEPINK LAUNCHES CHINA TOUR AS GRAND JURY INVESTIGATION INTO SINGHAM NETWORK FUNDING CONTINUES The ideological roots of the campaign extend to the Communist Party of the Philippines, founded by Sison in 1968. The United States designated the Communist Party of the Philippines and its armed wing, the New People's Army, as a foreign terrorist organization. In a Nov. 7 editorial, the party's official newspaper, Ang Bayan, urged Filipinos to organize "widespread protests" against Trump and to "reject and drive him out." The editorial accused Trump of advancing Pax Silica to strengthen American control over Philippine resources. The publication also reported that clandestine organizations associated with the National Democratic Front of the Philippines staged demonstrations. One teachers' group, KAGUMA, reportedly chanted, "Join the New People's Army!" The American campaign includes explicitly communist organizations, including the Workers World Party, a Marxist-Leninist organization, and the International Action Center. Separately, "Fight Back! News," published by the Freedom Road Socialist Organization, a Marxist-Leninist group that has organized many anti-ICE protests this year, republished an editorial from Ang Bayan criticizing Trump's Pax Silica initiative. CHINA ‘THROWING GASOLINE ON THE FIRE’ IN AI DATA CENTERS RACE, SAY LAWMAKERS The International League of Peoples' Struggle called for global protests under the slogans "Trump Out!" and "Reject Pax Silica!" The organization said groups planned demonstrations in 23 cities worldwide, including locations in the United States, Canada, Europe and Asia. American organizers identified planned actions in Los Angeles, Oregon, Washington, D.C., New York and Honolulu. In Ottawa, International League of Peoples' Struggle Canada, Anakbayan Ottawa, Migrante Ottawa and "Ottawa for Palestine" announced a demonstration for Wednesday outside the U.S. Embassy under the slogan "Shut the Pax Down!" In an April proposal to the U.S. State Department, Philippine officials outlined plans involving critical minerals, industrial infrastructure, investment and technology development. Protesters allege the project could displace Ayta Indigenous communities, expand mining, and strain electricity and water supplies. Philippine officials dispute allegations that the project would create a U.S.-controlled enclave or include the massive AI data centers described by activists. They say the development remains subject to Philippine law. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP As Trump arrived, demonstrations escalated. Reuters footage showed students marching with anti-Trump banners. SunStar reported more than 200 arrests during demonstrations in Metro Manila, while GMA News reported that activists condemned police dispersals and disputed the government's response.

articles.title: NSA's highly classified communications network disrupted by widespread outage
articles.summary: The National Security Agency's classified NSA Net faces an intermittent outage, with staggered arrivals preventing tens of thousands of logins at once.
articles.body: The National Security Agency's internal classified communications network is experiencing an "intermittent outage," but critical communications remain intact, a person familiar with the matter told Fox News Digital on Tuesday. The disruption affects a highly classified network known as NSA Net, which agency personnel use to communicate classified information internally. The latest impact at one of the nation's most sensitive intelligence agencies also comes amid a string of technology outages affecting major U.S. institutions, from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to Microsoft and major banks, raising fresh concerns about the reliability of critical communications infrastructure. DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE' CNN first reported the outage Tuesday, citing five people familiar with the matter. The agency has implemented staggered arrival times for personnel at NSA to prevent tens of thousands of employees from attempting to log into their computers simultaneously as officials work to address the disruption, the person familiar with the matter said. The issue appears to be technical in nature, according to the source, though the precise cause has not been established. Despite the disruption, the agency has not lost critical communications capabilities and has numerous backup facilities available to maintain operations, the source said. DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK The NSA, which is responsible for collecting and analyzing foreign signals intelligence, plays a central role in supporting U.S. intelligence and military operations. It remains unclear when the outage began or how long it will take to fully restore the affected network. Fox News Digital reached out to the NSA for comment. The disruption comes amid a string of high-profile technology outages over the last week affecting government systems and major businesses. On Friday, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop after a telecommunications failure disrupted aircraft communications and radar feeds. The agency said instability spread to 17 of its 22 air route traffic control centers before flights resumed later that evening. The disruption was attributed by the FAA to excessive data flooding its aging telecommunications network, potentially originating from two facilities in Texas and Arkansas. Officials said they had found no indication of a cyberattack. Federal authorities are separately warning of increasingly sophisticated cyber threats. In a Nov. 13 advisory, the FBI warned that hackers are exploiting an artificial intelligence-powered penetration testing framework known as ARTEX to automate attacks against organizations worldwide. The FBI said the technology has allowed some attackers to move from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. Microsoft previously linked the framework to a China-aligned hacking group's exploitation of a ConnectWise supply-chain compromise, which involved attempts to access more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 customer environments. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP There is no evidence linking the NSA disruption to the ARTEX activity or the other recent outages.

articles.title: Obama-appointed judge paves way to unseal Ilhan Omar search warrant in blow to Trump's DOJ
articles.summary: A federal judge in Washington, D.C., paved the way to unseal the criminal search warrant and related documents against Rep. Ilhan Omar.
articles.body: A federal judge in Washington, D.C. who has often ruled against the Trump administration dealt a blow to the Justice Department Tuesday, paving the way to unseal the criminal search warrant and related documents against Rep. Ilhan Omar. Judge James Boasberg, who was appointed to the bench by former President Barack Obama in 2011, asked the DOJ's attorneys to submit proposed redactions to the documents to the court by Friday, and said he plans to unseal some materials Monday. Any parts of the warrant or related materials that are not submitted with redactions on Friday will be released, he said. While criminal warrants aren't typically unsealed until after charges are filed, 15 media organizations and watchdog group Judicial Watch sued to obtain the warrant. They have argued that releasing the contents of the warrant is in the public interest. 'RADICAL LEFT LUNATIC' JUDGE TRUMP WANTED IMPEACHED TAKES UP ILHAN OMAR WARRANT FIGHT The plaintiffs argued specifically that it should be made public which statutes federal investigators think Omar may have broken. Boasberg signaled that he would not release the warrant application, which is a sworn statement submitted to a judge explaining facts and evidence that establish probable cause for issuing a warrant. The DOJ did not immediately return Fox News Digital's request for comment. Omar is facing a probe related to whether she or her father fraudulently filled out immigration paperwork in order for her to obtain citizenship. The Somali-born congresswoman said last week that she wasn't privy to what exactly the DOJ is investigating. During the raid, which was conducted by Homeland Security Investigations (HIS), Omar's personal cellphone, computer and passport were seized. Her DNA has also been obtained, and her sister, Sahra Noor, was questioned by investigators the week of the raid. FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE In a motion seeking to prevent the federal search warrant for the congresswoman’s home from being unsealed, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia referred to Omar as "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar…" and sources later told Fox News Digital that Ilhan Omar is not the congresswoman's "real name." That news caused speculation that Omar married her brother, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, to resurface. The pair married in 2009, and officially divorced in 2017. ILHAN OMAR APPEARS CLUELESS ON BASIS FOR FEDERAL PROBES: ‘YOU PROBABLY HAVE MORE DETAILS ON THAT’ Omar has not been charged with a crime and has repeatedly and categorically denied any wrongdoing. She has characterized the investigation as politically motivated, saying President Donald Trump is targeting her. But the DOJ under former President Barack Obama opened an investigation into Omar's marriage with Nur Said Elmi in 2016 — suggesting the nonpartisan nature of some of the inquiries into the Minnesota lawmaker. OBAMA BACKS ILHAN OMAR AMID PROBE, ACCUSES TRUMP ADMIN OF 'APPALLING' TARGETING IN LENGTHY STATEMENT The New York Times first reported that Obama's FBI and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) began the probe in the summer of 2016, and that officials "found some evidence that [the marriage] was fraudulent." The Times reported that the investigation concluded when officials decided the potential felony crime was past the statute of limitations. articles.title: Van Hollen’s bid to replace Schumer as leader is putting pressure on Democrats to take sides
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Senate Democrats elect their leader every two years behind closed doors and on a secret ballot. But this year’s race has burst into the pub...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Senate Democrats elect their leader every two years behind closed doors and on a secret ballot. But this year's race has burst into the public eye as Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen mounts an insurgent bid against New York incumbent Chuck Schumer.

The Dec. 1 contest has put Senate Democrats on edge and has forced what could become an ugly fight immediately after major victories in the midterm elections . It has also put the more moderate incoming Democrats in a tough spot, forced to take sides in a leadership race before they are even sworn into office.

Schumer, who recruited several of those moderate Democrats who helped win the majority, has said he has the votes to be reelected , and around 15 of the 55 elected Democrats in next year's caucus have said publicly that they will support him. Four Democratic senators have said they will support Van Hollen. Everyone else is staying quiet for now.

"Leave it to the Democrats," said Colorado Sen. John Hickenlooper, who flipped an imaginary coin when asked by reporters on Monday how he would vote. "We flipped nine seats, and the person who actually helps put it all together and do all that, and all of a sudden, there's a revolt."

Van Hollen, who is backed by progressive groups, says it's time for new leadership after Schumer's nearly decade-long tenure. While the two men align on most issues, Van Hollen says Democrats need to more aggressively push to end the Iran war and potentially even shut down the government next month, if necessary, to stop the flow of war funding.

"To deliver, we need new leadership," Van Hollen says. "This isn't about any one person – it's about answering that call."

Van Hollen is making his argument to the public as Schumer mostly keeps quiet and holds private his conversations with the senators who will decide his fate. Schumer shared his agenda for the next Congress in a caucus luncheon last week, laying out a plan to try to quickly pass legislation on healthcare and tariffs and to launch multiple investigations into President Donald Trump's Republican administration.

Asked about Van Hollen's challenge on Tuesday, Schumer said again that he's confident he has the votes.

"We are united together on lowering costs and ending corruption," Schumer said.

The unusually public race — the first contested election for Senate Democratic leader in decades — comes when Schumer has drawn intense criticism from the party's base. Some voters and progressive groups called for his removal in 2025 after he voted with Republicans to keep the government open and as they called for stronger opposition to Israel's war in Gaza .

Still, many in the caucus see the role not as a national figurehead but as an inside operator who can navigate intraparty politics and the 100-member Senate's arcane rules to pass legislation.

"I want to hear from any candidate what their vision is for the floor and managing the caucus," said Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, who was just reelected. He said he hasn't committed to either Schumer or Van Hollen.

Party leaders also spend much of their time fundraising and recruiting candidates — a particular interest for Schumer, who has been directly or indirectly in charge of the Senate Democrats' campaign arm for two decades.

Most Democrats don't want to reveal their vote

Returning to Washington on Monday for the first time since Van Hollen entered the race, most Democrats would not answer questions about who they would support. That included prominent progressives like Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren.

Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin appeared last week at a press conference with Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders , an independent who caucuses with Democrats, as he declared that he would not support Schumer. Van Hollen entered the race two days later, and Sanders immediately endorsed him. But Slotkin has not.

"I'm not saying anything," she told reporters on Monday.

Others like Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine defended Schumer while saying that they are still open to Van Hollen or someone else.

"Chuck delivered an amazing win," said Kaine. "Chuck knows Trump, and that will be really, really important going forward."

Still, Kaine said, "The voters are demanding change, so we have to figure that out as a caucus, and we're going to be able to. We're not afraid to have a discussion."

The eight incoming freshmen Democratic senators — nine if Mary Peltola wins the Alaska Senate race , which has still not been called — are set to alter the caucus next year. But only two have said how they will vote in the leadership election.

Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, both of whom were backed by progressive groups in their campaigns, say they support Van Hollen. Schumer supported both of their opponents in their primaries, though he eventually put $67 million into El-Sayed's competitive race.

El-Sayed said Tuesday that he likes Schumer and will work alongside him if he wins. But he said he thinks Van Hollen is the best person to take on affordability challenges and liberal priorities like Medicare for All .

"We have not seen an open Senate fight for leadership for a very long time," El-Sayed said at The Atlantic Summit in Washington. "This is healthy. It's good."

For some of the other freshmen, many of them moderates from Republican-leaning states, the decision could be more difficult. Some said during their campaigns that they wouldn't vote for Schumer. But it's unclear if any of them would back the more liberal Van Hollen.

In South Carolina on Tuesday, Sen.-elect Annie Andrews , a doctor, said that she is in conversations with both candidates and has been "sharing my plans to fix our healthcare system."

Incoming Iowa Sen. Josh Turek told reporters he's met with both Schumer and Van Hollen. He said he wants more specifics on how they will help rural families, overhaul campaign finance and ban lawmakers from trading stocks. Turek said he also wants to assess "who is going to put forth the most robust anti-corruption agenda."

Hawaii Sen. Mazie Hirono, who is backing Schumer, said that the caucus needs to hear more from the new senators who "have been through the fire to get here."

"I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard," she said. "They've got a lot of talent to bring to the table."

Associated Press writers Joey Cappelletti and Kevin Freking in Washington, Meg Kinnard in Columbia, S.C., and Hannah Fingerhut in Des Moines, Iowa, contributed to this report.

articles.title: ‘Squad’ member announces ‘Majority Priorities’ including reparations, abolishing ICE after blue wave
articles.summary: Rep. Ayanna Pressley dared President Donald Trump to veto reparations, Medicare-for-all and the abolishment of ICE as Democrats' new House majority sets up m...
articles.body:
Rep. Ayanna Pressley , D-Mass., unveiled a progressive legislative agenda for the incoming Democratic House majority Sunday, daring President Donald Trump to veto bold left-wing proposals ranging from reparations and Medicare-for-all to abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

"We need to show people what Democrats can do with our majority. Reparations. Abortion justice. Medicare for All. Abolishing ICE. Childcare. Paid leave. And more," Pressley wrote on X .

"If Trump wants to veto any of this, then the people will know exactly where he stands. And we won't stop fighting until we win."

The post included a graphic titled, "Rep. Ayanna Pressley's Majority Priorities," including the message: "TRUMP WANTS TO BE MR. VETO. LET'S PUT HIM TO THE TEST."

Beyond the policies highlighted in her post, the 13-point platform calls for extending temporary protected status (TPS) for certain immigrants, lowering housing and everyday costs, ending what she termed "Trump's Iran war," blocking weapons shipments, halting data centers and rooting out corruption.

Pressley's push comes nearly two weeks after Democrats won control of the House in the Nov. 3 midterm elections. While the party secured House and Senate majorities that will take office in January, Democrats remain well short of the two-thirds supermajority required in each chamber of Congress to override a presidential veto, setting the stage for messaging bills aimed at forcing Trump to reject progressive legislation.

At the top of Pressley's list is H.R. 40, the Commission to Study and Develop Reparation Proposals for African Americans Act, which Pressley reintroduced in January 2025 to examine the legacy of slavery and develop reparations proposals .

Other progressive lawmakers have pushed even further; in March 2026, Rep. Shri Thanedar, D-Mich., introduced separate legislation, H.R. 7927, to establish a federal commission to "study and distribute land reparations" to descendants of enslaved people.

The Department of Justice is involved in a lawsuit against Evanston, Illinois , for launching a reparations initiative that provides $25,000 in cash or housing-related financial assistance to eligible Black residents and descendants of Black residents. In 2019, Evanston became the first U.S. city to approve a municipal reparations plan , pledging $10 million over a decade funded by a local cannabis tax.

While progressive Democrats have long championed reparations, the issue has repeatedly drawn pushback from moderate members of the party who view it as a political liability.

A DOJ official told Fox News Digital that while the agency "does not comment on the legislative priorities of members of Congress or speculate about future legislation, any legislation that allocates public benefits based on race is unconstitutional and debating such bills would be a waste of Congress's time."

"Our lawsuit challenging Evanston's reparations program is about the Constitution and federal civil rights law," the spokesperson said. "As alleged in our filing, the program provides housing-related financial assistance based on race, which violates the equal protection clause and the Fair Housing Act. The department's position is set out in court filings.

"The department enforces federal civil rights laws, which protect all Americans equally regardless of race. We will continue to do so."

Pressley's renewed call to abolish ICE drew a sharp rebuke from the Trump administration.

A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson told Fox News Digital Pressley should be grateful the administration has removed "dangerous criminals from her district."

"America's brave ICE agents put their lives on the line every day to enforce U.S. law and arrest criminal illegal aliens, including gang members, rapists and murderers," the spokesperson said.

"Representative [Pressley] should be thanking our law enforcement for removing these dangerous criminals from her district — NOT vilifying law enforcement. This type of rhetoric is contributing to a more than 1,600% increase in assaults against them as they put their lives on the line.

"Since day one, DHS law enforcement has been delivering on President Trump's promise to the American people to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens, including murderers, rapists, pedophiles, gang members and terrorists," the spokesperson added.

"Nearly 60% of ICE arrests are of illegal aliens charged or convicted of a crime in the U.S. More than 3 million illegal aliens are out of the country and counting. Our message is clear: If you come to our country illegally, we will find you, we will arrest you and we will deport you."

DHS also warned that anti-ICE rhetoric from elected officials has coincided with a surge in targeted violence against federal immigration officers.

"Attacks and demonization of ICE law enforcement is wrong. Because of smears like this, our ICE officers are now facing a 1,600% increase in assaults, a 3,300% increase in vehicle attacks and an 8,000% increase in death threats," the spokesperson said.

Pressley and Thanedar did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

articles.title: Senior US official undercuts CNN’s alarming Iran ‘dirty bomb’ report: ‘It’s not new’
articles.summary: President Donald Trump warned Iran would pay a price "no country has ever paid" if a dirty bomb threat to Washington, D.C., proves real, amid divided assessments.
articles.body: A senior U.S. official is challenging a new report on Iran developing plans for a "dirty bomb" attack on Washington, D.C., which drew a warning of overwhelming retaliation from President Donald Trump this week. The prospect of Iranian-directed violence on American soil has shadowed U.S. security officials for decades. From a plot to bomb a Washington restaurant to assassination schemes targeting former officials and dissidents, Tehran has repeatedly sought ways to reach its enemies inside U.S. borders. "I’m not sure why this was leaked because it’s not new," a senior U.S. official told Fox News' Jennifer Griffin in response to the report. "Iran is very aspirational, but not suicidal. If they were to attack D.C. or any other U.S. city it would cause us to have a full out war with them. Their friends would not come to their aid." CNN reported this week that U.S. intelligence indicated Iran was developing potential plans to target senior Trump administration officials in Washington with a radiological device or chemical weapon. BESSENT MOVED TO MILITARY BASE AS IRAN THREATS EXCEED ‘ADVANCED STAGE,’ OFFICIAL SAYS Sources described the planning as an effort to develop options rather than evidence of an imminent attack, with officials divided over whether Tehran could or would execute it. "We’re looking into it," Trump said in Manila on Tuesday when asked about the new report. Pressed on whether Washington faced an imminent threat, he warned: "Well, if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before." "I hope it’s not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," the president added. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said, "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland." Iran could make a dirty bomb, but would need someone inside the United States with the expertise to handle the materials and carry out an attack, said Andrea Stricker, deputy director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ nonproliferation program. A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives with radioactive material, spreading contamination without producing a nuclear explosion. U.S. authorities have spent nearly two decades building defenses against that possibility. DHS launched its Securing the Cities program in 2007 to help local agencies detect and deter nuclear and radiological threats, including dirty bombs, beginning in the New York City region. "Making a radiological dispersal device would be within Iran’s know-how, as well as a chemical weapon," Stricker told Fox News Digital. Iran’s chemical weapons program dates back to the 1980s. "More recently, they've been looking at how to weaponize chemical weapons like fentanyl and disperse them through the air," Stricker said. Fentanyl can suppress breathing to the point of respiratory arrest. "I think for an attack using chemical weapons like this, they would probably want to go with something rudimentary. Industrial scale chemicals like chlorine would be easy to obtain," she added. IRAN-BACKED TERROR SUSPECTS PLOTTED ATTACK ON US TROOPS USING VANS PACKED WITH FUEL, DOJ SAYS Rather than risk transporting hazardous materials into the country, Tehran could look to obtain them here, she said. "They may want to simply try to steal them or procure them from inside the United States. That would probably ease their task," Stricker said. But the technical demands would complicate Iran’s reliance on hired criminals to execute its operations. "In the past, they've used sort of everyday criminals for hire to execute some of their other plots, and luckily we foiled a lot of these," she said. articles.title: Democrats with 2028 ambitions say their party still must prove itself to win the White House: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: In today’s edition, Natasha Korecki files a dispatch from a recent gathering of jubilant, but forward-looking, Democrats in Denver.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Natasha Korecki files a dispatch from a recent gathering of jubilant, but forward-looking, Democrats in Denver. Plus, Peter Nicholas and Jared Perlo dig into President Donald Trump’s relationship with former (and possibly future?) Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. — Adam Wollner Democrats with 2028 ambitions say their party still must prove itself to win the White House Analysis by Natasha Korecki DENVER — They came to celebrate, to gloat and to reflect. But mostly, they came to launch the next chapter. The convening of some 3,500 Democrats at the “What’s Next” conference organized by Majority Democrats here last week made a couple of things clear. First is the most obvious: While the party was still riding high after the midterms, it couldn’t wait to move into a 2028 presidential posture. Governors, members of Congress and former Cabinet secretaries took turns testing messages onstage and taking a spin before reporters. The second thing may be refreshing news to their party: Democrats across the board seemed to understand that they can’t rest on their laurels and need to use their newly won power to come through in a big way and quickly. Otherwise, in two years they’ll be out again. Speaker after speaker conveyed that the shifts that swept them into office were temporary. They realize that Americans dislike both parties, they just dislike Republicans more right now. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who is exploring a White House run, said that to sustain trust into 2028, Democrats had to reverse President Donald Trump’s unpopular policies by ending tariffs and blocking Iran war funding. “We all have to marshal every tool we have that the people just put in our hands,” Shapiro said. “That means ending this reckless war and these tariffs that drive up our prices and drive away our allies. Bringing accountability to the sweetheart deals, the mass agents, the use of American weapons on open seas and across the globe.” Meanwhile, Democrats like Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas said that they would work with Trump if it meant getting a key policy priority over the goal line. “Our job as elected leaders is to deliver real things for people, so if slapping Trump’s name on it and putting it in gold letters would get it through, hell yes, I would do that,” Slotkin said. “I’m going to be measured and graded on what actually happens for people in Michigan.” Of a possible 2028 bid, Slotkin said, “I am looking at it seriously.” Other Democratic presidential contenders, including Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona, Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey and Rep. Ro Khanna of California, were also part of the fray in Denver. For his part, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg urged his party to work with speed once they took control of Congress in January. “I am hopeful that instead of getting gummed up in a 1,000-page bill that takes six months to put together, we come out of the gate with a rapid fire of things that will put money back in people’s pockets,” Buttigieg told reporters. And Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia said that if Americans were to believe that Democrats were fighting for them, they had to put money into their pockets. “Only a nation that is spiritually broken, only a people that were already deeply disappointed could have elected the likes of Donald Trump twice,” Warnock said. “And so this fight is a moral fight. We must raise worker wages and the index of our moral imagination. We must heal the land. And we can.” Related reads: Hakeem Jeffries endorses lowering Medicare age, adding benefits and universal coverage for kids, by Sahil KapurDemocrats weigh how far to go with their newfound power in the states, by Adam Edelman Trump had a mutually beneficial relationship with Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, one he’s reluctant to let go By Peter Nicholas and Jared Perlo Before his downfall at Nvidia, former CEO Jensen Huang had ingratiated himself with President Donald Trump in ways that paid off handsomely for both. Huang was the sort of business titan Trump tends to cultivate. He was the charismatic force behind one of the great corporate success stories of the 21st century and had grown unimaginably rich along the way. And Trump was the sort of president that Huang’s company needed. The Trump administration accommodated Nvidia by easing certain restrictions imposed by former President Joe Biden, allowing the company to sell some of its older-generation chips to China that had once been banned. Huang’s future is now uncertain. He resigned from Nvidia amid accusations that he had an affair with a Chinese government asset. Trump isn’t forsaking him, and this week, he took a step toward rehabilitating Huang in the realm of public opinion. For a transactional president, that could prove useful down the road. Since his swearing-in, Trump has courted a stable of high-tech billionaires who offer both cachet and money for his pet renovation projects and partisan political causes. Huang said today that he would be “honored” to return to his job as CEO of Nvidia if the company’s board of directors decided to bring him back. Republicans also announced that Huang had agreed to sit for an interview with several House committees about whether Nvidia’s sales to China may have endangered U.S. national security. Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. articles.title: Unclear if Illinois stadium bill will be introduced during fall veto session this week
articles.summary: Illinois lawmakers returned to Springfield this week for the fall veto session, with discussions expected to focus on several key issues, including potential...
articles.body:
Illinois lawmakers returned to Springfield this week for the fall veto session, with discussions expected to focus on several key issues, including potential legislation aimed at keeping the Chicago Bears in Illinois and additional funding sought by Chicago Public Schools.

The first week of the fall veto session is scheduled for three days; although House Speaker Emanuel "Chris" Welch has already canceled Thursday's session. As a result, much of the work is expected to take place behind the scenes, including continued negotiations on legislation related to a potential Bears stadium project.

House members convened briefly Tuesday before breaking to caucus so they could discuss priorities for the week and for their return in early December.

One major issue under discussion is legislation intended to prevent the Bears from relocating to Indiana. The bill is still being drafted, and it remains unclear whether it will be introduced during this week's session. Conversations with the team have continued, lawmakers said.

"What's important for us is making sure that we can socialize whatever is in the legislation with the members of the House and the Senate, and do it in a way that is very clear that the House and Senate are holding hands on this," said state Rep. Kam Buckner, D-Chicago and speaker pro tempore.

The Bears are considering property they purchased nearly four years ago in Arlington Heights. More recently, separate development proposals have been pitched for a domed stadium at the former U.S. Steel site along the lakefront on Chicago's Southeast Side and at the former Michael Reese Hospital site in Bronzeville.

"Every proposal I've seen for Chicago site I think has a lot of promise. But here's the thing to keep in mind: We want the Bears to pay for the stadium. The Bears have said they would. We want to take them up on that offer. If the Bears are going to pay for the stadium, they are going to have a lot of say on where the stadium goes," said state Sen. Bill Cunningham, D-Chicago.

Hammond Mayor Tom McDermott said he still believes Hammond presents the strongest business case for the Bears after numerous meetings and discussions with team representatives. Discussions between the Bears and Illinois lawmakers have continued, but team representatives are not expected to be in Springfield during this week's veto session.

Also Tuesday, Chicago Public Schools CEO Macquline King and other school advocates traveled to Springfield to urge lawmakers to provide additional education funding.

The request includes funding to cover the $150 million incorporated into the district's budget that CPS does not currently have without assistance from the state.

"We've had great conversations with all of the leaders that we've touched base with, and I believe that they all collectively want the same thing for Chicago Public Schools and the school districts," King said.

Lawmakers, however, have indicated that additional education funding is not expected before next spring. The delay could lead to budget reductions or layoffs, according to King.

The debates are unfolding as House Democrats prepare to elect a new speaker to replace Welch. Welch was pressured not to seek another term following criticism of his handling of a sexual harassment claim involving former state Rep. Harry Benton.

Eight House Democrats are currently seeking support for the leadership post, including Kam Buckner, Eva-Dina Delgado, Jehan Gordon-Booth, Jay Hoffman, Ann Williams, Marcus Evans, Camille Lilly and Will Davis. Several are members of Welch's current leadership team. The new speaker will need 60 votes to be elected, with the vote expected to take place in January.

articles.title: DOJ watchdog notes surge in misconduct complaints
articles.summary: A Tuesday report reviewing the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) top challenges noted a surge in professional responsibility complaints filed against the department’s prosecutors. The report from DOJ’s Office of Inspector General focused on a number of managerial issues, concluding that those facing the DOJ’s Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) are among the top challenges facing…
articles.body:
A Tuesday report reviewing the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) top challenges noted a surge in professional responsibility complaints filed against the department’s prosecutors.

The report from DOJ’s Office of Inspector General focused on a number of managerial issues, concluding that those facing the DOJ’s Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) are among the top challenges facing the department.

“OPR reported receiving 2,081 professional misconduct complaints in FY [fiscal year] 2026, compared with 1,666 in FY 2025, 1,346 in FY 2024, and 1,085 in FY 2023—an increase of approximately 54 percent in 2 years,” the report states.

The report notes OPR opened 10 full-scale investigations out of the complaints made this year, finding professional misconduct in nine of the cases.

OPR has limited staffing to review the complaints, the report noted.

“These results demonstrate that OPR has continued to resolve substantial workloads despite its limited size. However, the Department faces risk in its oversight capacity if OPR’s staffing levels are insufficient to manage the workload generated by the Department’s thousands of employees,” the report states.

The report notes OPR also received 50 new FBI whistleblower retaliation complaints.

The review comes as DOJ has lost a record number of staff , while a number of its prosecutorial moves have come under fire — including cases brought against several perceived foes of the president.

The surge in complaints is even more pronounced when looking at the earliest data provided under the Biden era, doubling since fiscal 2023.

The Office of Inspector General stressed that the OPR’s work was paramount as the DOJ faces continued questions about its integrity.

“This challenge encompasses, but is broader than, public perception,” the report states.

“Integrity and fairness are operational requirements for a law enforcement institution, not merely matters of public image.”

articles.title: Sean Duffy’s $50 billion demand for air travel fixes is met with yelling and skepticism in Congress
articles.summary: The Trump administration’s request for $50.1 billion in new FAA funding after a nationwide ground stop is running into skepticism from both parties in Congress.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Trump administration’s request for $50.1 billion in new Federal Aviation Administration funding after a nationwide ground stop strangled air travel is running into skepticism from both parties on Capitol Hill. The funding request was suddenly increased from $30 billion after the hourslong ground stop Friday caused delays and cancellations for passengers across thousands of flights. The formal funding ask was conveyed in a Tuesday letter signed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who refused to apologize or accept responsibility for the failure, blaming it on predecessors and Congress. The letter, cosigned by FAA chief Bryan Bedford and White House budget director Russell Vought, stated the money was needed “to deliver a truly world-class air traffic control network.” After publicly reproaching Congress for the failure last week, Duffy met privately with Senate Republicans on Tuesday to make his case on Capitol Hill. The closed-door briefing was contentious. The transportation secretary was “yelled at” by multiple Republican senators during his briefing, according to a person in the room who was not authorized to speak publicly about the private discussion. When it was over, Senate Republican leaders and Duffy notably held their news conferences separately. Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., stopped short of endorsing the full funding figure, saying only that the GOP is unified around the belief that “safe skies is an incredibly important priority.” “We will see what the traffic will bear, what’s achievable,” he said, calling it a “discussion to be had” on the dollar amount. Duffy met with only Republicans on Tuesday, not Democrats — even though the regular government funding process requires bipartisan support. And Democrats were left wanting a better explanation, particularly as Duffy has pointed fingers at them. And members in both parties noted that President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” included $12.5 billion for air traffic control that still has not been fully used up. “Look, we have not been given the answers. They have not come clean,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., told reporters on Tuesday. “At his first press conference, all Duffy did was attack Democrats, and he asked for $50 billion when they haven’t even spent the $12 billion we’ve given to them. I have little faith in them.” Facing Republican questions on the matter, Duffy insisted that the $12.5 billion was insufficient for the specific upgrades he deemed necessary in this situation. Other Democrats are vexed by the FAA funding request. “I generally support the idea of investing in air traffic control, but $50 billion sounds like an awfully round number,” said Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, who’s poised to become majority whip and also sits on the Senate Appropriations Committee. The issue is wrapped up in a larger debate about funding the government ahead of a Dec. 11 deadline to avoid another shutdown. Congress could either reach a deal by then on new funding, punt it to next year with a stopgap bill, or fail to act and allow a shutdown. Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, said air traffic control is “absolutely not a partisan issue” and that Congress will work to make sure that any funding is “paid for in a responsible way.” Republicans are also considering a party-line “reconciliation” bill to approve military funding without the need for Democratic votes; Democrats are likely to resist additional military funds unless the Iran war comes to an end. Other provisions could be added to such a bill — if it materializes before Republicans lose control of Congress. Thune indicated Tuesday that it is still an open question, as Republicans would need to pass a budget resolution by Thanksgiving to pull it off. It would be a long, arduous process requiring near-total GOP unity in both chambers, and it would need to begin soon in order to finish this year. Duffy said he’s agnostic on how the funds get passed when asked by NBC News why he only met with Republicans on Tuesday. “I have met with Democrats. I’ve spent hours on the phone with Democrats. Get along with them well. They understand this issue,” Duffy said Tuesday, speaking to reporters separately after meeting with GOP senators. “I’m not going to tell them how to do their work, but I’m telling everybody what we need. I’m making a nice ask, and I’m going to let them work their process.” One of the Democrats whom Duffy spoke to was House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely next House speaker. “I appreciated the conversation,” Jeffries told reporters. “There are still more questions than answers in terms of what happened, why it happened, how do we prevent it from happening again.” Jeffries added that he wants a briefing on the FAA ground stop and other recent outages, saying: “These developments are troubling, and it’s unclear if it’s all infrastructure-related or whether there’s some malignant activity.” When asked about Duffy’s $50.1 billion request, outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said Republicans would work with the administration to fund “as much of that as we can.” He pointed to the $12.5 billion already approved for FAA modernization and did not specify a timeline or whether Congress would pursue a supplemental funding package.

articles.title: Nvidia: China fears Jensen Huang scandal could shut it out of US AI tech before Xi-Trump summit
articles.summary: China worries the scandal could ramp up pressure on the US  to further restrict the sale of advanced chips.
articles.body:
Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.

For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.

Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.

US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.

The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.

For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.

Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.

Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.

Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something much bigger.

Democrats, who will control Congress come January, have made their position clear. Last Wednesday top Democrat Ted Lieu told Politico the Trump administration had been "1,000%" too deferential to Nvidia, putting national security at risk, while fellow Democrat Zoe Lofgren suggested Congress would now be more likely to restrict sales of AI chips to China.

The BBC has approached the White House for comment.

Beijing's foreign ministry had described the spy claims as a "smear against China".

"The US should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives to find pretexts for imposing technological blockades," spokesperson Mao Ning said last week.

The ministry also seemed keen to keep the meeting on track, saying the two countries had kept "close communication regarding interactions between the two heads of state".

For the last year, Trump and Xi have been seeking to stabilise relations after a damaging tariff war that almost brought trade between the two countries to a standstill.

The Trump administration's decision to permit sales of advanced Nvidia H200 chips to China in late 2025 was seen as evidence that both sides were searching for areas of co-operation, even while competition intensified.

It was a rare move given Washington had spent years trying to limit China's access to the most advanced chips.

Many in the US have long viewed these chips as a national security issue, arguing they could strengthen China's military and surveillance capabilities. Jensen Huang, who rejects that claim , advocated lifting bans on the export of high-performing chips to China. Beijing argues the restrictions are an attempt to contain its rise.

History has taught Beijing and Washington that spy scandals rarely remain confined to the intelligence world.

Analysts in China already see echoes of an incident in 2023 when a suspected surveillance balloon drifted through the skies over the US before an American fighter jet shot it down. Beijing insisted it was a civilian meteorological airship that had strayed off course.

But a planned trip by then US Secretary of State Antony Blinken was cancelled and communication between the two governments deteriorated sharply.

The incident showed how quickly a security dispute could overwhelm diplomatic efforts and push relations into a deep freeze.

"The mere passage of a balloon sent American public opinion and politicians into a state of high alert, as if a "Chinese threat" were looming directly overhead," said the state media outlet, the Global Times this week as it made a direct comparison with the Nvidia scandal.

"No-one on the US side has ever apologised or taken responsibility for the genuine damage this caused to US-China relations," it added.

The state-run outlet also questioned why the Nvidia story had emerged so soon after "the hard-won detente" between Beijing and Washington, following a meeting between the two countries' leaders in September.

"Is someone behind the scenes pushing an agenda and stirring up confrontation?" it asked.

Both Trump and Xi have significant incentives to keep talking.

China's economy remains under pressure and is increasingly reliant on exports. Xi needs trade to keep flowing and this meeting is a key stepping stone to replacing the current trade truce that is due to expire in January.

Meanwhile Trump has repeatedly touted his close relationship with Xi and argued that maintaining dialogue is essential to managing competition between the two powers.

The US president is in his last two years and faces an uphill struggle to pass domestic legislation after the midterms. To counter this, he could be looking for some foreign policy wins.

He may also hope for Xi's help to end the war in the Middle East.

Neither side will want to be discussing intelligence concerns and technology controls instead of trade, investment and economic co-operation.

The summit is also being carefully choreographed by Beijing to show off its technological prowess in Shenzhen - a deeply symbolic choice of city.

It's home to some of the country's biggest tech companies and has become a showcase for Beijing's ambitions in AI and advanced manufacturing.

Also, given Washington's tighter restrictions on advanced chips, Beijing has options for retaliation.

One of its most powerful tools is its dominance of key rare earth minerals. China processes much of the world's supply for materials that are used in everything from electric vehicles and smartphones to military equipment.

Analysts have long warned that technological restrictions can trigger a cycle of retaliation in which each side reaches for its strongest economic leverage.

That would shift the current trend of US-China relations from engagement back towards mutual suspicion.

Republican lawmakers and other prominent conservative figures are growing skeptical over the wave of recent technology outages .

A day earlier, J.P. Morgan Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo experienced disruptions, preventing customers from accessing their bank accounts. United Airlines experienced a system outage also on Monday that resolved later in the evening.

articles.title: White House blasts 'Trumpcare for All' pitch from far-left El-Sayed who called president 'unserious fool'
articles.summary: White House slammed Abdul El-Sayed's "Trumpcare for All" pitch, warning the Medicare for All plan would threaten Americans' existing health coverage.
articles.body: The White House blasted far-left Michigan Democrat Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed's pitch to President Donald Trump to embrace "Trumpcare for All," warning that the Medicare for All proposal would threaten Americans' existing health coverage. "The Radical Democrats’ socialist proposal for a government takeover of healthcare should really be called ‘Medicare for None’ as it destroys access to the life-saving care Americans rely on daily," White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster told Fox News Digital. The sharp response came after El-Sayed, who recently called Trump an "unserious fool," posted a 16-second video Tuesday urging the president to embrace the progressive proposal. BERNIE SANDERS THINKS MEDICARE FOR ALL BILL COULD PASS, 'NOT ABSOLUTELY CERTAIN' TRUMP WOULD VETO "I think there is a responsibility that we have to engage with [Trump] as the unserious fool that he is," El-Sayed said during a recent appearance on "Pod Save America," according to earlier Fox News Digital reporting. Despite those remarks, the senator-elect struck a more conciliatory tone in his latest appeal. "Donald. Habibi. Midterms were rough. I get it," El-Sayed said in the video posted Nov. 17, addressing Trump with the Arabic term "habibi," commonly translated as "my dear" or "my beloved." "Trumpcare for All. It's really popular. People really want healthcare. You can put your name all over it." EL-SAYED ADMITS FREE HEALTHCARE MEANS PAYING 'A LITTLE BIT MORE IN TAXES' REGARDLESS OF INCOME The video featured a mock "Trumpcare" card and an AI-generated image depicting Trump as Jesus Christ, which El-Sayed, a Muslim, referenced while urging the president to embrace socialized, taxpayer-funded healthcare. "Donald, this is your chance to heal the sick (like in that one AI image. You know the one)," El-Sayed said. The White House instead pointed to Trump's efforts to lower prescription drug prices, contrasting those policies with the single-payer system advocated by El-Sayed. "President Trump is focused on taking on the special interests that are driving up the costs of healthcare for all Americans including through his historic efforts to ensure American patients never pay more than those in other developed nations for all prescription drugs, which has already saved Americans well over $1 Billion," Schuster said. MAJORITY OF AMERICANS BROADLY REJECT SOCIALIST IDEOLOGY EVEN AS FAR LEFT SURGES TO POWER "The President will continue delivering real results that lower costs and put Americans first, while Democrats push ideas that have devastated economies and ruined healthcare quality anywhere they have been implemented." The administration also cited a U.S. Council of Economic Advisers' analysis estimating that Medicare for All would increase the federal budget deficit by approximately $47.4 trillion between 2027 and 2036 in the absence of additional taxes or revenues. The White House also cited a CEA projection that Medicare for All would shift large numbers of Americans away from employer-sponsored insurance and into a new government-run coverage system. Medicare for All, a sweeping single-payer health care proposal championed by Democratic socialists, would replace much of the nation's private health insurance system with federally financed coverage. Supporters argue it would guarantee coverage, while critics warn of substantial tax increases and massive federal spending. El-Sayed's public appeal was not his first attempt to recruit Trump to the idea. During a CNN appearance earlier this month, the incoming senator suggested that the president could attach his name to a universal health care proposal. "Donald, if you're watching, we can put your name on it. I know you like to put your name on stuff," El-Sayed said, according to a Nov. 10 social media post by CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins. The unusual overture follows a contentious Michigan Senate race in which El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Democrat also mocked Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Rogers during his election victory remarks, adding to the contrast between his earlier criticism of the administration and his latest invitation to collaborate. El-Sayed is scheduled to take office Jan. 3, 2027. El-Sayed's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
