articles.title: US officially a measles endemic country
articles.summary: Presented by Coalition to Strengthen America’s Healthcare {beacon} Healthcare Healthcare The Big Story US officially a measles endemic country The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) confirmed Tuesday that it was withdrawing the U.S.’s measles elimination status, ending more than two decades of what is considered to be one of the greatest public health achievements in…
articles.body:
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) confirmed Tuesday that it was withdrawing the U.S.’s measles elimination status , ending more than two decades of what is considered to be one of the greatest public health achievements in modern history.

The U.S. met with PAHO’s Measles and Rubella Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission for a three-day, closed-door meeting last week.

“The commission concluded that the endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn, a recommendation which I have accepted,” Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO’s director, said during the briefing Tuesday.

The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000 and has held onto that for more than 25 years. But the past two years have seen close to 8,000 measles infections and roughly a dozen related deaths. This year has been the worst in terms of transmission in more than 30 years.

Following the Tuesday announcement, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. wrote on social media, “We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”

But federal health officials don’t seem pressed to change the current approach to the ongoing measles outbreaks across the country in light of PAHO’s announcement.

Erica Schwartz, director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has previously said losing elimination status won’t lead to changes in the federal response.

“We know where transmission is occurring and we’ve invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities,” Schwartz said on Tuesday. “Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.”

The countries are now expected to present their corrective action plans to PAHO in the coming weeks. Canada lost its own measles elimination status one year ago and began working with PAHO to regain that distinction.

Last month its multi-jurisdictional outbreak was declared over, and the country will need to prevent 12 months of sustained domestic transmission to regain its elimination status.

articles.title: Pakistani man gets more than 27 years in U.S. prison for assassination plot that he said was steered from Iran
articles.summary: Possible targets included politicians like Donald Trump, Joe Biden or Nikki Haley, according to testimony in the trial of Pakistani businessman Asif Merchant.
articles.body: NEW YORK — A man who admitted trying to get a U.S. politician killed — and said Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard drove him to it — was sentenced Tuesday to nearly three decades in prison. Asif Merchant, a Pakistani businessman, had faced the possibility of life in prison for what the judge called an exceptionally serious crime. Possible targets of the thwarted plot included then-candidate and now-President Donald Trump, then-President Joe Biden or then-candidate and former U.N. Ambassador Nikki Haley, according to trial testimony. “Not many charges … are more serious than the contemplated, targeted killing of a U.S. president or other senior government official,” said U.S. District Judge Eric Komitee, a Trump appointee. Merchant, 48, shifted in his chair but otherwise showed no visible reaction when he was sentenced to a little more than 27 years. One of his lawyers, Avraham Moskowitz, said after court that Merchant plans to appeal but was grateful that the judge turned down prosecutors’ bid for a life term. “I think what it shows is that our judiciary remains independent, thankfully,” Moskowitz said. Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement that Merchant was “justly sentenced.” The sentencing capped a remarkable trial about an alleged Iran-driven plan to kill a prominent U.S. political figure in the thick of the 2024 campaign season. The Iranian government has denied trying to kill U.S. officials. Merchant, who was convicted earlier this year of murder for hire and attempted terrorism, declined to speak at his sentencing. But at his trial, he bluntly told jurors that he researched Trump rally locations and spoke of carrying out an assassination at a political rally, using objects on a hotel napkin to illustrate the scenario for an acquaintance. Merchant then lined up people he thought were hit men and paid them $5,000 in cash that he’d borrowed from a relative. He testified that he was just playing along with instructions from a Revolutionary Guard intelligence operative in order to protect relatives in Iran. Merchant said he figured that U.S. authorities would foil the plan, that he would cooperate and that he might get immigration help as a reward. U.S. law enforcement was, indeed, onto him: The supposed killers-for-hire actually were undercover FBI agents, tipped by the acquaintance who saw Merchant’s napkin demonstration. Merchant was arrested in Texas while packing for a flight back to Pakistan on July 12, 2024, a day before an unrelated attempt on Trump’s life in Butler, Pennsylvania. “This plot was incompetent from the very beginning,” defense lawyer Christopher Neff said in court on Tuesday. “Mr. Merchant’s participation was half-hearted.” Merchant worked for Pakistani banks for decades and then got into businesses ranging from car sales to banana exports, and he traveled periodically to the U.S. for work and to see relatives. He also traveled to Iran for Shiite Muslim religious pilgrimages and visits with kin. After meeting a Revolutionary Guard operative several years ago, Merchant imagined intelligence work would be exciting and profitable, and he feared for his relatives’ safety if he defied the powerful paramilitary, according to his defense. “My family was under threat, and I had to do this,” Merchant testified in March. He said his handler named Biden, Haley and Trump as potential targets. Prosecutors challenged Merchant’s claim that he acted under duress. They noted that he had shared anti-American and anti-Trump social media posts after the U.S. killing of top Iranian military leader Qassem Soleimani in 2020, during Trump’s first administration. Merchant’s defense portrayed the posts as venting, and Neff insisted that his client wasn’t an extremist or inclined to turn his beliefs into violence. But Assistant U.S. Attorney Sarah Winik countered that Merchant did “the most extreme thing you can do: Plot the assassination of a government official.” The judge said he believed Merchant had some concern for his family but also was “highly motivated to do harm to this country.”

articles.title: Ecuadorian fishermen sue Trump administration after surviving boat strike
articles.summary: More than a dozen Ecuadorian fishermen have filed a lawsuit against the U.S. government after surviving a military drone attack against their boat in the Pacific Ocean earlier this year, claiming they were wrongfully targeted for drug trafficking. The lawsuit, filed Monday by 16 fishermen, alleges that two explosive-laden drones struck their fishing vessel on…
articles.body:
More than a dozen Ecuadorian fishermen have filed a lawsuit against the U.S. government after surviving a military drone attack against their boat in the Pacific Ocean earlier this year, claiming they were wrongfully targeted for drug trafficking.

The lawsuit, filed Monday by 16 fishermen , alleges that two explosive-laden drones struck their fishing vessel on March 17 as the crew returned from a two-week fishing trip near the Galapagos Islands.

The explosions set the boat ablaze and caused it to sink, forcing the fishermen to jump into the ocean. Two crew members suffered severe burns, including one whose leg was burned to the bone, according to the 17-page complaint.

The Trump administration’s strikes on drug-trafficking vessels in the Pacific were part of Operation Southern Spear , which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said was created to quash “narco-terrorists” in the Western Hemisphere.

The U.S. forces have carried out 72 strikes against alleged drug-trafficking vessels that have killed at least 244 people since September 2025, according to a tally by The New York Times.

The fishermen say they had no ties to drug trafficking and that Ecuadorian naval authorities had boarded and inspected their vessel just hours before the attack, finding no drugs or evidence of criminal activity.

After escaping in emergency boats, the men approached a nearby vessel, where they say armed U.S. personnel restrained them with zip ties and placed plastic hoods over their heads. They allege that they were forced to stand barefoot on a hot deck for 24 hours without food and with little water.

They were subsequently transferred to El Salvador in what they described as “deplorable conditions” before returning to Ecuador later that month.

The lawsuit is challenging the legality of the Trump administration’s broader maritime campaign, arguing that Congress never authorized the strikes and that no armed conflict exists to justify the use of lethal force against suspected drug traffickers, particularly on March 17.

The U.S. military has not acknowledged carrying out the March attack. The Pentagon and Coast Guard previously denied involvement in the reported attacks.

“We have no knowledge of, nor were Department of War forces involved in, the incidents described in those reports,” a U.S. Southern Command spokesperson said in June.

Apesar dos ótimos resultados em provas apenas ao prestar a atenção nas aulas, Hilton Dias de Oliveira , de 18 anos, tem dificuldade para sentar e estudar, o que aumenta o desafio na preparação para vestibular. " É diferente, você precisa sentar e estudar e isso eu não costumo fazer ", resume.

As distrações geram um problema extra para Gabriel Ferreira Carnielli , de 16 anos, especialmente com matemática. "Eu acabo errando porque deixo passar algum detalhe". O mesmo acontece com João Pompêo de Camargo Ibrahim , de 17 anos.

Em comum, os três estudantes têm superdotação , condição que dividem com cerca de 5 mil pessoas no Brasil e que, segundo as matrículas registradas pelo Ministério da Educação, tem crescido nas escolas da região de Campinas. A lém disso, que impõe altas expectativas nesta época de vestibular.

O g1 conversou com especialistas que explicam que, apesar do estereótipo, entender rapidamente um conceito não significa, necessariamente, conseguir resolver todas as questões de uma prova. 🧠 Nesta reportagem você vai ver:

Por que superdotação não garante nota alta no vestibular

Altas habilidades, superdotação e QI alto

📚 Esta reportagem compõe o projeto Vestibulou , uma iniciativa do g1 Campinas para divulgar informações relacionadas aos principais vestibulares e ajudar na preparação dos estudantes.

A lei que institui a Política Nacional para Estudantes com Altas Habilidades ou Superdotação define como uma condição do neurodesenvolvimento associada a características como potencial intelectual elevado, curiosidade intensa e facilidade para aprender. A descrição também considera o chamado "hiperfoco" em temas de interesse e características como sensibilidade e intensidade.

De acordo com a psicóloga e presidente da Associação Superdotação Campinas, Sabrina Silva, a superdotação não é um transtorno, mas sim uma forma de funcionamento. “É um cérebro que processa informações de forma diferente, com mais rapidez e com maior sensibilidade. É um organismo, que funciona de forma diferente”, explica.

“A superdotação não está relacionada apenas ao quanto uma pessoa é capaz de aprender ou realizar, mas também à forma como ela percebe o mundo, processa informações e estabelece conexões entre ideias. Muitas vezes, a pessoa superdotada identifica padrões, faz associações e compreende conceitos complexos com uma rapidez ou profundidade que chamam a atenção”.

“Mas isso não significa que ela saiba tudo ou tenha facilidade em todas as áreas. Significa que seu funcionamento cognitivo pode apresentar características diferenciadas”.

não existe um único padrão de funcionamento capaz de definir todas as pessoas superdotadas;

cada indivíduo tem seu próprio perfil, com habilidades, dificuldades e necessidades diferentes;

compreender a superdotação exige olhar para além dos resultados e reconhecer como essa pessoa pensa, aprende, sente e interage com o mundo.

Ainda segundo a especialista, a neurociência vem investigando essas particularidades e apontando associações entre a inteligência elevada e diferenças na organização e na comunicação entre redes cerebrais.

Dessa forma, o diferencial estaria, então, não apenas na quantidade de conhecimento que a pessoa consegue acumular, mas também na maneira como seu cérebro organiza e relaciona aquilo que aprende.

Isso pode se refletir na curiosidade intensa, na busca por explicações, na percepção de detalhes e na capacidade de conectar assuntos aparentemente distantes.

'Você precisa sentar e estudar, e isso eu não costumo fazer'

Hilton Dias de Oliveira, de 18 anos, é superdotado e relata dificuldade na preparação para o vestibular — Foto: Isadora de Paiva/g1

O modo de funcionamento do cérebro dos superdotados reflete na maneira como eles se preparam para o vestibular. A repetição de exercícios, a necessidade de decorar certos conceitos e fórmulas e a escrita da redação podem ser desafiadoras para esses estudantes . É o caso de Hilton Dias de Oliveira, de 18 anos, que estuda arquitetura na PUC-Campinas.

“Tenho dificuldade de sentar e estudar. As aulas no ensino médio eram interessantes, eu ia muito bem sem estudar. Só de prestar atenção, eu já passava com notas acima da média. Mas para o vestibular é diferente, você precisa sentar e estudar e isso eu não costumo fazer”, conta o jovem.

No ano passado, Oliveira ficou em 19º lugar na lista de espera da USP e agora quer cursar arquitetura em São Carlos.

“A parte de redação foi a que mais pesou no meu caso. Não é meu interesse ficar escrevendo, escrevendo. Sei que é algo importante, mas é difícil para mim essa repetição. E para uma boa redação é prática. Além disso, tem a parte da memorização, de química, por exemplo, de ficar decorando tipos de carbono. Isso também era algo difícil”.

Até mesmo a matemática pode ser um bicho de sete cabeças para os superdotados . Gabriel Ferreira Carnielli, que tem 16 anos, está na 2ª série do ensino médio, conta que tem dificuldade ligadas à atenção, que muitas vezes escapa.

“Temas relacionados à proporção, por exemplo, são complicados para mim. Eu acabo errando porque deixo passar algum detalhe”, conta Gabriel, que busca vaga no curso de física, na Unicamp.

O estudante João Pompêo de Camargo Ibrahim, de 17 anos, também diz que a distração é o que mais o prejudica na hora de resolver as questões. “Tenho estudado quase todos os dias por meio de exercícios e aulas. Além da escola, faço cursinho e pretendo cursar Ciência da Computação na USP ou na Unicamp”.

“Gostaria de entrar em qualquer uma das duas, mas a minha principal dificuldade relacionada aos estudos é o erro de questões por distração.”

A psicóloga e neuropsicopedagoga Patrícia Schneider, integrante da diretoria da Mensa Brasil — organização mundial de alto QI —, explica que uma pessoa superdotada não vai apresentar, necessariamente, um desempenho escolar excepcional .

“Ter altas habilidades não significa ser excelente em tudo, aprender tudo sozinho ou necessariamente apresentar um desempenho escolar excepcional. Podemos ter um jovem com raciocínio muito acima da média e, ao mesmo tempo, com dificuldades de organização, gestão do tempo, tolerância à repetição, ansiedade diante de provas ou até lacunas importantes de conteúdo”, destaca.

Schneider explica que muitos desses jovens passam boa parte da vida escolar aprendendo com muita facilidade e, justamente por isso, não precisam desenvolver métodos de estudo consistentes. No entanto, quando estão diante de uma situação altamente competitiva, como o vestibular, podem descobrir que compreender rapidamente um conteúdo é diferente de ter repertório, treino, constância e estratégia .

Por isso, para ela, na preparação para o vestibular é fundamental olhar para o perfil individual daquele estudante e entender:

quais são suas áreas de maior potencial;

sua capacidade de planejamento e autorregulação;

“Costumo fazer uma analogia: é como alguém que sempre correu muito rápido, mas nunca precisou treinar para uma maratona. Ter velocidade ajuda, evidentemente, mas uma prova longa exige também preparo, estratégia, resistência, conhecimento do percurso e capacidade de administrar o próprio ritmo”.

'Superdotados são pessoas, não máquinas'

As especialistas lembram que a pressão sobre o superdotado nessa fase da vida também pode afetar o desempenho nos vestibulares . “O superdotado também é gente, não é uma máquina de calcular. É uma pessoa que pode cometer erros também. Cria-se uma imagem de uma pessoa que faz conta rápido e não é isso. É preciso quebrar esse estereótipo, porque isso é prejudicial”, lembra Carnielli.

Schneider diz ainda que a obrigação de corresponder ao potencial depositado sobre o superdotado — junto de outros fatores como ansiedade, perfeccionismo, autoexigência e medo de fracassar — pode gerar uma carga muito grande, minguando a capacidade real daquele indivíduo.

“Uma identificação de altas habilidades não pode se transformar em uma sentença de desempenho. Ela deveria servir para compreendermos melhor aquela pessoa e oferecermos condições adequadas para que desenvolva seu potencial — e não para aumentar a cobrança sobre ela”.

A psicóloga Sabrina Silva explica que uma pessoa já nasce superdotada , “ela não treina e vira superdotada”. Por isso, diz que não costuma usar o termo altas habilidades , que pode ser associado à superdotação, “porque habilidade você pode treinar e conquistar. Superdotação não é treino, é um funcionamento”, explica.

Ela destaca ainda que existem diversos caminhos sendo estudados, principalmente com a ajuda da neurociência, para entender o cérebro do superdotado e compreender quais fatores determinam essa característica. “Existem linhas de pesquisa que avaliam por meio de ressonância funcional, outras avaliam o volume do cérebro, a hiperconectividade, a eficiência da substância branca e da mielinização, e a rapidez dos impulsos elétricos”.

“O que a gente sabe e espera, dentro do futuro das pesquisas, é essa integração da neurociência, esse olhar funcional e, principalmente, essa busca para compreender por que e como esse cérebro, tanto estruturalmente quanto anatomicamente, funciona. É um caminho em que tem se investido bastante para ter essas respostas”, pontua.

O QI (Quociente de Inteligência) é um dos fatores analisados por uma dessas linhas de pesquisa. Para a psicometria, o superdotado é aquela pessoa que tem um QI acima de 130. No entanto, outras vertentes defendem um QI acima de 120. Para chegar ao QI, é preciso realizar uma série de testes e questionários conduzidos por psicólogos e neuropsicólogos.

“É um mito imaginar que altas habilidades significam apenas um QI elevado. A avaliação é muito mais ampla e precisa considerar o indivíduo em sua totalidade: seu funcionamento cognitivo, sua trajetória de desenvolvimento, suas habilidades, criatividade, interesses, realizações, contexto educacional e aspectos socioemocionais”, destaca a neuropsicopedagoga da Mensa Brasil.

O Ministério da Educação e os Núcleos de Atividades de Altas Habilidades/Superdotação (NAAH/S) no Brasil usam como maior referência o psicólogo norte-americano Joseph Renzulli, que define o comportamento superdotado não como um escore fixo de QI, mas a partir da intersecção de três dimensões fundamentais: capacidade acima da média, criatividade e comprometimento com a tarefa .

articles.title: Fachin recebe nesta quarta relatório da PF sobre ministros no caso Master e deve avaliar modelo para definir próximos passos | G1
articles.standfirst: Elementos reunidos por delegados podem levar presidente da Corte a enviar casos de colegas para análise da PGR, medida que tem apoio nas duas alas.
articles.summary: Elementos reunidos por delegados podem levar presidente da Corte a enviar casos de colegas para análise da PGR, medida que tem apoio nas duas alas.
articles.body:
O presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), ministro Edson Fachin , deve receber nesta quarta-feira (18) os relatórios produzidos pela Polícia Federal, com menções a ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) e parentes no caso Master. O formato do material pode ser decisivo para a definição dos próximos passos da crise na Corte.

As providências que serão adotadas cabem ao presidente do Supremo, que se encontra na noite desta quarta-feira (18) com o diretor-geral da Polícia Federal. A reunião está prevista para depois da sessão da Corte.

O relatório deve detalhar menções e citações sem avançar sobre condutas criminosas ou não . Os documentos chegam ao STF quando a primeira fase da Operação Compliance Zero, que investiga as fraudes do Master e suas conexões, completa um ano.

Segundo interlocutores, há pelo menos dois caminhos em análise por Fachin: envio para parecer da Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) ou análise interna, na seara disciplinar e administrativa, por exemplo.

Se estiverem presentes os elementos necessários, ou seja, que indiquem infrações penais, os documentos devem ser encaminhados para avaliação da PGR.

Na Procuradoria, a indicação é de que caberá ao grupo montado pelo procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet, a análise do que foi apontado pela Polícia Federal contra os magistrados, avaliando se há ou não elementos para abertura de investigação.

Isso seria feito antes de uma decisão do plenário do Supremo, que não precisa seguir automaticamente o entendimento da Procuradoria para determinar o início de uma apuração.

O envio à PGR foi adotado após a PF elaborar, por determinação do ministro André Mendonça, relatório sobre menções a Moraes no caso Master, o que instalou uma crise institucional sem precedentes no Supremo.

O relatório apontou Moraes como interlocutor de 52 mensagens do banqueiro, que demonstravam apreensão com as investigações e pedidos de interferência . Também foram apontadas uma suposta análise e edição por parte do ministro de um contrato de R$ 130 milhões , assinado entre o Banco Master e o escritório de advocacia Barci de Moraes, de Viviane Barci.

Mendonça pediu que o plenário decidisse sobre investigar o colega. Moraes nega diálogos com Vorcaro e afirma não ter cometido irregularidades.

No primeiro relatório sobre Moraes, a Procuradoria já se manifestou, no Supremo, a favor de que o documento seja arquivado sob o argumento de que a sua produção foi irregular.

A análise pela PGR tem apoio de ministros das alas de Moraes e de Mendonça. O encaminhamento dos casos para a PGR, além de dar respaldo ao Supremo para decidir diante de uma análise técnica, ainda daria tempo para novas investidas para uma composição interna — apontada ainda como de difícil solução.

Outra possibilidade é que os relatórios sejam tratados como questão administrativa, portanto, o que poderia configurar uma questão disciplinar. Isso levaria inicialmente a uma análise interna, uma espécie de filtro sobre o que foi levantado pela PF e depois as questões até poderiam ser enviadas para a PGR.

Se considerar que os dados não são suficientes, o presidente da Corte pode até mesmo pedir que a PF refaça ou aprofunde uma análise técnica.

Na última semana, Andrei chegou a telefonar para Fachin para tratar do modelo dos relatórios. A ligação ocorreu após o desgaste interno na PF por conta do afastamento dos delegados da PF afastados de suas funções, após participaram da elaboração de relatórios sobre o envolvimento de ministros com o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro.

O comando da PF determinou que os documentos fossem refeitos . O material foi requisitado por Fachin ao diretor-geral da PF.

Dos 10 ministros do Supremo, há citações, em graus diferentes, de pelo menos seis ministros ou parentes — além de referências a ministros do Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ) e do Tribunal Superior do Trabalho (TST).

A entrega dos relatórios deve pressionar ainda mais o presidente do STF. Uma questão em aberto seria também estabelecer como e em quais as condições para participação de citados em eventuais julgamentos.

Presidente do Supremo Tribunal Fedreal (STF), ministro Edson Fachin — Foto: Antonio Augusto/STF

As ligações de ministros do STF com o caso Master começaram em abril de 2025, quando a colunista Malu Gaspar, do jornal "O Globo", revelou a contratação do escritório da mulher do ministro Alexandre de Moraes pelo Banco Master para representação em algumas ações.

Em dezembro, foi publicado que o contrato era de cerca de R$ 130 milhões e, neste ano, a PF apontou que o ministro foi interlocutor ao menos de 52 mensagens de Vorcaro, inclusive no dia em que foi preso.

Depois, surgiram negócios que envolviam o ministro Dias Toffoli com fundos do Banco Master na sociedade de um resort da família do ministro no Paraná , o que levou o ministro a deixar a relatoria do caso Master e a se declarar suspeito para analisar questões da investigação.

Em setembro deste ano, surgiram mensagens que citavam envolvimento do ministro Nunes Marques com Daniel Vorcaro, inclusive com suposto favorecimento pessoal do filho do ministro e do filho do ministro Luiz Fux, por suposto pedido de ajuda em um processo.

Em relação ao ministro André Mendonça, foi divulgada uma foto com advogado de Vorcaro, um encontro com o banqueiro e um pedido de investigação de uma possível relação entre o Banco Master e o Instituto Iter — ligado ao ministro.

Também foi identificada a contratação de Chiquinho Feitosa, ex-cunhado do ministro Gilmar Mendes, por Vorcaro, além de uma reunião e tentativas de aproximação.

Todos os ministros e familiares negam irregularidades ou envolvimentos com Daniel Vorcaro.

Daniel Vorcaro — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

articles.body:
Judge vacates ESA review underlying offshore mining

A court ruling this week is throwing a wrench into the Trump administration’s bid to open up mining off the coast of American Samoa.

© Fili Sagapolutele, Associated Press file

Judge Jill Otake, a Trump appointee, ruled that the administration did not adequately consider the potential impacts of offshore mining during its Endangered Species Act review.

Her ruling noted that the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) “only considered the preliminary effects of the lease sale and did not even attempt to consider” other activities such as actual mining.

She wrote that the agency’s “cramped, expedited, informal consultation is apparently unprecedented” and vacated the letter determining that no further Endangered Species Act consultation was required for the lease sale.

The ruling does not appear to explicitly vacate the lease sale itself, however, and it’s not immediately clear whether the Trump administration will attempt to move forward with the sale, which had been scheduled for Thursday.

A spokesperson for the Marine Minerals Administration said that the agency, which would carry out the lease sale, “is aware of the opinion” in an email to The Hill. “We are currently working to address the issues raised in the court’s opinion.”

However, in a separate but related case challenging the lease sale itself rather than the review, Otake wrote that if she vacates the review but the Trump administration moves ahead with the lease sale, “any bidders for the leases will be on notice that the Court has determined that NMFS violated the Endangered Species Act …regarding the proposed leases.”

articles.title: Trump administration permanently pulls funding from LA homeless agency over mounting fraud allegations
articles.summary: The Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority will give up about $150 million in federal funding under a HUD settlement, with LA County managing the money.
articles.body: The Trump administration on Monday announced a landmark settlement to permanently cut the scandal-plagued Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority (LAHSA) off from federal funding, citing overwhelming evidence of fraud and years of mismanagement that wasted taxpayer dollars. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) said the agreement requires LAHSA to relinquish about $150 million in federal funding and permanently sever its ties to HUD's homelessness funding programs by the end of 2027. "Organizations that are complicit in this fraud and waste will not get one penny more of federal funding," Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said in a statement. LA HOMELESSNESS FRAUD CASES EXPOSE DEEPER PROBLEM THAN STOLEN MILLIONS, OVERSIGHT HAWK WARNS Los Angeles County will take over managing the funds used to combat homelessness, while HUD will closely monitor how the money is spent, according to officials. The agreement, executed Thursday, resolves a lawsuit filed by LAHSA challenging HUD's June decision to suspend further funding to the agency. According to HUD, investigators found that LAHSA received more federal homelessness funding than any other jurisdiction in the nation, taking in nearly $1 billion in taxpayer dollars over the last five years. LA REAL ESTATE VET COMES AT MAYOR BASS WITH RECEIPTS OVER DAMNING HOMELESSNESS REPORT: 'SHE DOESN'T GET IT' "Los Angeles remains the epicenter of the nation’s drug-fueled homelessness crisis. On top of this, their failure has enabled record homelessness fraud," HUD said. HUD Secretary Scott Turner said LAHSA had spent years funneling federal funding to organizations without proper oversight. "Taxpayers will no longer bankroll an organization that fails to deliver for the Americans it was created to serve," Turner said in a statement. HUD’S HOMELESSNESS REFORMS PUT HUMAN LIVES AHEAD OF HOUSING BUREAUCRACY "For years, American taxpayers have been sending billions of dollars to Los Angeles to house the homeless and other vulnerable Americans. The result? Fraud and corruption," Scott Brady, executive director of the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, added in a statement. HUD added that it is committed to ending what it called the "harmful" "Housing First" policy, which provides permanent housing to homeless individuals without requiring them to meet preconditions such as sobriety or participation in therapy. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Under a new Treatment First approach, individuals will likely need to participate in addiction or mental health treatment and demonstrate progress toward recovery to qualify for and maintain housing assistance. "HUD is rejecting the addiction-fueled depravity seen from LA’s Skid Row to New York’s ‘Boulevard of Broken Dreams’ and moving to Treatment First to restore lives of self-sufficiency," Turner previously said. The settlement comes as HUD reports a 6.3% decrease in homelessness, the largest recorded decline, during the first year of Trump's administration. "President Trump’s actions to secure the border, get criminal illegals off our streets and restore safety to our communities drove a historic decrease in homelessness," Turner previously said.

articles.title: 'Mob Wives' star Renee Graziano rejects NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani as 'not my choice' in public safety clash
articles.summary: Former "Mob Wives" star Renee Graziano criticized NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani and criminal justice policies on Tomi Lahren's podcast, as Mamdani defended his NYPD overhaul.
articles.body: Former "Mob Wives" star Renee Graziano criticized New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani during a discussion on public safety, saying he is "not my choice." Speaking on the "Tomi Lahren Is Fearless" podcast, Graziano told Lahren that Americans shouldn’t be attacked for wanting their streets to be safe and said she disagrees with Mamdani on "probably everything." "I don't agree with him on a lot of things. Probably everything, I don't agree with him," Graziano said. "He's not my choice. And if he is for other people, God bless them. He would not be the person I voted for." Graziano’s comments came after Lahren raised concerns about New York’s no-cash bail policies and Mamdani’s move to disband the NYPD’s protest unit. Under changes announced by Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch on Monday dissolving the Strategic Response Group (SRG), the unit’s counterterrorism functions will be folded into the Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau, while a new civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD) and specialized NYPD teams will handle protest response. MICHAEL RUIZ: NEW YORK'S GUTTED POLICE UNIT WAS MORE THAN A PROTEST SQUAD Graziano, who said she tries "not to pay attention" to Mamdani, criticized the justice system, arguing that criminal justice policies have allowed repeat offenders to be released. "You're letting men out that raped women, and they get out and they rape women. They're out the door 20 seconds later, and they're still committing crimes," she said. Graziano said she’s faced criticism on social media for calling for public safety, including being labeled "MAGA" by commenters. "I had made a statement. One day on my Instagram, I said, ‘Can we make America safe again?’ And I got attacked viciously," Graziano said. "‘Oh, you're a MAGA, you're this, you're that, you're Trumper,’ or you're this or that," Graziano added. "First of all, who I decide to pick is my business. I don't need to tell anybody, it's my choice. But I would never attack a person because they don't like this color or they don't like that. I would never do that. And I've experienced that across the board. And all I said was make it safe. I didn't say make it great. I said, make it safe." JIM CAVIEZEL SAYS A SURREAL ENCOUNTER WITH JESUS CONVINCED HIM TO STAR IN 'THE PASSION OF THE CHRIST' Graziano also argued that Americans need to be fully committed to the country, saying those who don't want to be here "can leave." "You know, don’t half step in America. We are America. We are a beautiful country. So either we're all in or we're out. And if you don't want to be here, you can leave. That's how I truly feel." At a news conference Tuesday, Mamdani defended his decision to dissolve the SRG, describing counterterrorism and protest response as "fundamentally different responsibilities." MAMDANI PREPARES TO FULFILL PROMISE TO AXE NYPD UNIT RESPONSIBLE FOR CONTROLLING PROTEST VIOLENCE "New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat. I made this promise over the course of the campaign, and I'm proud to be fulfilling this promise," Mamdani said. Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani's team for comment but did not immediately hear back. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital’s Anders Hagstrom contributed to this report.

articles.title: White House pulls Trump’s FDA pick Heidi Overton on eve of Senate panel vote
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's FDA pick, Heidi Overton, saw her nomination pulled one day before a Senate committee vote, a White House official confirmed.
articles.body: The White House pulled Heidi Overton’s nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration, a White House official confirmed to Fox News, one day before a Senate committee vote. President Donald Trump hailed Overton as a "ROCKSTAR" in August when he picked the physician and White House advisor to succeed Marty Makary, who resigned in May. At her September confirmation hearing, Overton clashed with Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., as he pressed her to endorse universal healthcare as a human right. TRUMP TO NOMINATE DR HEIDI OVERTON AS NEXT FDA COMMISSIONER Senate health committee Chairman Bill Cassidy, R-La., pointed to Overton’s appearance alongside Trump in the Oval Office as Trump signed an executive order calling for changes to childhood vaccine recommendations, including splitting up the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. Cassidy said there was no scientific evidence for Trump’s suggestion that the combined shot could be "quite lethal" and warned the remark could discourage vaccination. TRUMP SURGEON GENERAL PICK BACKS MMR VACCINE, REJECTS LINK BETWEEN CHILDHOOD VACCINES AND AUTISM "Yes, Senator, the MMR vaccine is safe and effective," Overton told Cassidy. When he pressed her on what she would do if Trump asked her to disregard the FDA’s safety standards, Overton said she would give the president her best advice and follow the legal requirements for reviewing individual products. Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., asked Overton directly whether Trump was wrong. Overton reiterated that the vaccine was safe and effective and called it the best tool available during the measles outbreak. Sen. articles.title: What is Trump hoping to achieve at APEC meeting in China?
articles.summary: US president expected to meet with Chinese leader for third time this year; hold trilateral summit with Putin.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, this week, where he is expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and hold a three-way meeting with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

A Trump-Xi meeting on the sidelines of the economic summit, which includes 21 Pacific Rim member economies, would be the third time the two superpower leaders have met this year.

The prior meetings – with Xi hosting Trump in Beijing in May and Trump hosting Xi at the White House in September – were heavy on ceremonial pomp, as both leaders sought to portray a sense of stability in the consequential relationship, but light on meaningful breakthroughs.

Experts predicted a similar approach in Shenzhen, as topics of AI regulation, trade and the self-ruling island of Taiwan will again loom large.

The summit comes just days after Democrats won commanding control of both chambers of the US Congress, a shift that will likely serve as a major check on the US president in his final two years in office. Beijing, meanwhile, is increasingly looking beyond the Trump era to see what comes next.

“Trump will work to strengthen his rapport with Xi, but the meeting is unlikely to produce any substantive breakthroughs,” Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser on US-China relations at Crisis Group, said.

As for Russia, Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yury Ushakov told reporters on Monday that “the significance and symbolism” of the meetings between the three superpower leaders “are hard to overestimate”.

Neither side has yet released a formal agenda for an expected Trump-Xi meeting, although the White House announced plans for the two countries to support each other at APEC and at the G20 summit in Florida in December.

“The two countries agreed to build a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity,” according to a White House statement.

As in previous meetings, AI regulation is set to loom large. Both the US and China, as industry leaders, have faced pressure to jointly agree to safeguards on the transformative technology.

In September, both sides pledged to set up a mechanism to quickly communicate AI-related incidents and to hold a dialogue on emerging risks.

Still, the Trump administration has repeatedly downplayed the need to integrate developmental guardrails. Following the White House meeting, Trump said the US would “not be putting on brakes” on the AI industry.

Speaking at a National Committee on US-China Relations event last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said both sides “expect to exchange best practices for evaluating and testing advanced models before their release, and for keeping human judgment firmly in command of this technology”.

“As we do so, we should harbour no illusions about the differences between the United States and China,” he said. “And our approach to every challenge, likewise, will not always converge.”

The recent resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which followed revelations that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, will also loom large over any Trump-Xi meeting, even if it is not directly addressed.

Huang’s close relationship with Trump, including accompanying the US president to Beijing during his May visit, and his ties to alleged spy Alice Huang have renewed questions about the influence he exerted over the US government as he pushed to ease restrictions on the sale of advanced AI chips to Beijing.

Trump administration Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has faced particular scrutiny, including from prominent members of the Republican Party, over his reportedly lax enforcement of export controls related to China.

“Trump will be under enormous pressure from Congress and members of his own administration to raise the scandal and warn Xi that their relationship could suffer if Trump concludes that Xi has been deploying Huang and other prominent business executives to sabotage US artificial intelligence efforts,” according to Crisis Group’s Wyne.

Still, some experts expect it to have little bearing on his interaction with his Chinese counterpart.

Gabriel Wildau, managing director at the advisory firm Teneo, told Al Jazeera last week that Trump “shows no sign that he intends to disrupt the current US-China rapprochement”.

The Reuters news agency reported on Friday that US officials said Trump is not expected to raise the issue of Alice Huang with Xi.

China has denied Alice Huang was working as a spy on its behalf.

Trump has already bucked longstanding US policy on Taiwan during his recent meeting with Xi.

Following the Beijing summit in May, Trump told reporters he had discussed US arms sales to the self-governing island, which Beijing claims as its own, “in great detail” with the Chinese president.

The US has provided arms to Taiwan since 1979 as mandated under the Taiwan Relations Act. But under the 1982 Six Assurances document, Washington has not consulted with China on such sales.

In a subsequent Fox News interview, Trump also referred to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” with China. He has since held up approval of a $14bn arms package earmarked for the island.

The language “invites Beijing to expect something in return for each future approval”, Bonnie Glaser and Noah Munk of The German Marshall Fund of the United States (GMF) wrote in a recent analysis.

“The more successful that bargaining appears, the more Beijing will press it, and the more it will treat the next notification as a concession from Washington rather than a routine measure under the Taiwan Relations Act,” they wrote.

For its part, the White House has defended the delay, citing limited production capacity, particularly amid the US-Israel war with Iran, as well as the delicate nature of the US-China trade truce.

Democratic control of Congress, and general bipartisan support for Taiwan, could see pressure increase on the issue in Trump’s final two years in office.

“Today, the results of the midterm elections are on balance favourable for Taiwan,” Robert Sutter, a professor of international affairs at George Washington University, wrote recently for the ThinkChina publication.

Taiwan, a member of APEC, will be represented at the summit by Acer Group founder Stan Shih.

US-China trade relations took a nosedive at the start of Trump’s second term, with the US president initially launching 10 percent tariffs on China for allegedly failing to crack down on the trade of fentanyl precursors.

By April, additional US tariffs on Chinese goods had reached 145 percent , while China’s retaliatory tariffs on US goods reached 125 percent.

Agreements to bring down the temperature faltered until Trump and Xi agreed to a yearlong truce in Busan, South Korea, in October of last year. The deal was extended through January 10, 2027, following Xi’s White House visit in September.

A particular issue has been US access to China’s rare earth minerals, which was severely restricted. Still, a recent analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) found that US imports of China’s rare earth minerals during the first 11 months of the agreement remained 75 percent lower than prior to the escalation.

“The recurring challenge is the persistent gap between China’s diplomatic commitments and actual export volumes,” the analysts wrote. “Despite successive agreements in Switzerland, London, and South Korea intended to restore supplies, shipments of controlled rare earth materials to the United States remain approximately 75 percent below pre-restriction levels.”

US agricultural exports were also hard hit during the trade war, an issue for farmers that resonated during the midterm elections. In recent meetings, China has agreed to buy 25 million metric tonnes of US soya beans, as well as what the White House has described as $17bn per year in US agricultural products in 2026, 2027, and 2028.

Those purchases have also lagged behind the commitments.

The most significant outcome of this year’s APEC summit may be the three-way meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin.

Such a meeting would likely be seen as a massive boon for Putin.

“By sitting down with the leaders of the world’s two most powerful countries in a trilateral format, Putin will be recognised as a major player on the world stage rather than a pariah,” Ryan Hass, a China expert at the Brookings Institution, wrote in a recent analysis.

Xi, in turn, would “bask in the glow of China serving as the convener and agenda-setter for how China, Russia, and the United States will relate to each other”.

The benefit for Trump, who the White House says will focus on denuclearisation efforts, remains less clear, according to experts.

“A trilateral meeting would showcase the extent to which both Trump and Putin seek to curry favour with Xi,” Crisis Group’s Wyne said.

“It would also further unnerve US allies and partners that fear Trump’s openness to an informal ‘G2’ or ‘G3’ arrangement,” he said, referring to a global realignment that bypasses other world powers.

articles.title: Senate Intel Vice Chair Warner says AI contributing to network outages
articles.summary: Senate Intelligence Committee ranking member Mark Warner (D-Va.) alleged Tuesday that AI contributed to several high-profile system outages this week, arguing industries are under pressure to quickly identify and fix security issues the technology can easily exploit. “What appears to be happening instead is a consequence of how quickly artificial intelligence is changing the cybersecurity…
articles.body:
Senate Intelligence Committee ranking member Mark Warner (D-Va.) alleged Tuesday that AI contributed to several high-profile system outages this week, arguing industries are under pressure to quickly identify and fix security issues the technology can easily exploit.

“What appears to be happening instead is a consequence of how quickly artificial intelligence is changing the cybersecurity landscape,” Warner wrote in a Tuesday statement.

“AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change.”

Warner’s statement followed high-profile outages at major U.S. banks, Microsoft and, most notably, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) — the latter of which led to a rare nationwide ground stop.

AI can help organizations respond to emerging cybersecurity risks, but cybercriminals can use these same capabilities to scale and refine their attacks, a Harvard cybersecurity panel said in June of 2025.

Warner acknowledged there was no indication the FAA and bank outages this week were the “result of a cyberattack, foreign interference, or some coordinated effort” but stressed he hoped the disruptions served as a “wake-up call.”

“It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” the senator wrote.

A preliminary investigation into the FAA’s nationwide ground stop pointed to a router in Arkansas and a radar facility in Texas that caused a data flood, forcing personnel to shut down the system. The stop lasted for several hours Friday and led to thousands of flight delays and cancellations.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a press conference Saturday the FAA and FBI “ don’t have clarity yet ” on the root cause behind Friday’s outage, though he later attributed the telecommunications issues to a contractor’s wire replacement.

“I promise all of you that when I know what happened with that router injecting that overload into our system, I will most definitely share that with you,” the transportation secretary continued. “If we were subject to a hack, we will share that with you as well, but all of my intelligence partners are telling me that wasn’t the case.”

articles.title: Kelly knocks Hun Cao’s analogy about food shortages on Navy ships
articles.summary: Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) knocked acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao’s confirmation hearing analogy on Navy vessel food shortages, implying the comparison undermined the reports of poor conditions aboard ships docked in the Middle East. During the hearing, Cao compared reports that certain sailors aboard the USS George Washington and the Boxer Amphibious Ready Group were…
articles.body:
Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) knocked acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao’s confirmation hearing analogy on Navy vessel food shortages, implying the comparison undermined the reports of poor conditions aboard ships docked in the Middle East.

During the hearing , Cao compared reports that certain sailors aboard the USS George Washington and the Boxer Amphibious Ready Group were losing as much as 45 pounds to his kids “opening up the refrigerator door and saying, ‘There’s nothing in here.’”

Kelly, a former Navy pilot, almost immediately interrupted Cao, remarking that “somebody doesn’t lose 45 pounds just because they don’t like the options” — adding he didn’t “think that’s a fair assessment.”

In a Tuesday social media post after the proceedings concluded, Kelly continued his criticism, writing, “Losing 45 pounds is more serious than just not liking the food.”

“Our sailors are being asked to serve thousands of miles from home for months at a time,” the senator continued. “We have a responsibility to make sure they have what they need to do their jobs and stay healthy.”

The Guardian reported in August that three naval families had told the outlet their relatives deployed in the middle east had lost 20 to 30 pounds due to insufficient nourishment. One mother the publication her son was “emaciated” while others discussed low-quality drinking water and scarce mental health support.

While the nominee has the support of Senate Armed Services Committee Chair Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), Democrats on the panel remain skeptical.

Democratic senators pressed Cao during Tuesday’s hearing over grueling conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln during its record deployment, during which eight service members attempted suicide .

When asked about the suicide attempts, Cao referred to the incidents as “eight mitigations we’re able to mitigate.”

Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) responded in a heightened tone, asking Cao not to “call attempted suicide mitigations. That is such an insult.”

“When you say it’s mitigation, you’re compartmentalizing something that is clearly a mental health failure,” she said. “The fact that a service member, a sailor, went overboard is beyond a mitigation.”

articles.title: Murkowski calls midterms ‘a direct pushback to President Trump’
articles.summary: Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) said Republicans’ staggering midterm losses were were a clear rebuke of President Trump from voters. “I think what you saw was a pushback on some of the administration’s policies, and a direct pushback to President Trump,” Murkowski said Tuesday during an appearance on Alaska Public Media’s “Talk of Alaska.” The moderate…
articles.body:
Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) said Republicans’ staggering midterm losses were were a clear rebuke of President Trump from voters.

“I think what you saw was a pushback on some of the administration’s policies, and a direct pushback to President Trump,” Murkowski said Tuesday during an appearance on Alaska Public Media’s “Talk of Alaska.”

The moderate Republican pointed to key issues that influenced voters at the polls, including concerns about the economy exacerbated by an unpopular war in Iran, and corruption in Washington.

“In addition to affordability, people were concerned about what they believe to be levels of corruption … or issues they felt where unfair advantage was being taken by those in power,” she said.

Murkowski, who has frequently broken with Trump, said she was initially relieved by Trump’s reaction to the abysmal election results, noting that he had not repeated his past claims without evidence of widespread election fraud — though he later cast doubts on the results a week later.

“There was no suggestion that the elections were ‘stolen’ or ‘rigged’ or what have you, and I thought that that was a positive,” she said.

But that optimism appeared to be short-lived. Murkowski pointed to Trump’s move to tap Stephen Miller, a longtime adviser and architect of Trump’s aggressive immigration agenda, as White House chief of staff.

“It does send a pretty direct signal, I think, when you put a person like Stephen Miller in as chief of staff,” she said, arguing the appointment of the immigration hard-liner showed Trump has not taken the election results seriously.

Murkowski also weighed in on Alaska’s closely watched Senate race, where former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) has built a sizable lead over incumbent Rep. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), though the contest remains uncalled two weeks after Election Day.

Peltola held nearly 50 percent of first-choice votes as of Monday, compared with nearly 46 percent for Sullivan, according to Decision Desk HQ . Should Peltola win the race, it would give Democrats another Senate seat and expand their newly won majority to 56.

Murkowski, who endorsed Sullivan’s reelection bid, said Tuesday that she would be happy to work with Peltola.

“I’ve worked well with him, but I also worked well with Mary Peltola when she was Rep. Peltola in the House,” Murkowski said, referring to Peltola’s previous tenure in Congress. “If she is certified and elected, I will look forward to working with her just as I did before.”

articles.title: Mamdani's luxury second home tax hits $500M milestone despite thousands of exemptions
articles.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani's pied-à-terre tax has billed wealthy second-home owners more than $500 million, even as tax bills fell far below initial estimates.
articles.body: New York City has billed wealthy second-home owners more than $500 million under Mayor Zohran Mamdani's controversial pied-à-terre tax, even as the number of homeowners receiving bills fell far below initial estimates. "We've billed more than $500 million to owners of second homes worth more than $5 million," Mamdani wrote Tuesday on X. "That's half a billion dollars to invest in a City that works for all New Yorkers," he continued. According to information provided by city officials, the New York City Department of Finance mailed approximately 7,500 tax bills — a sizable drop from the roughly 17,000 initial notices sent to property owners over the summer. APPEALS COURT HANDS MAMDANI LEGAL WIN ON NYC LUXURY SECOND-HOME TAX Officials also said roughly 8,900 exemption applications were granted, while approximately 1,600 extension applications were denied. The surcharge is a key part of the mayor's agenda to raise taxes on wealthy New Yorkers and help close the city's budget gap. Despite the smaller number of bills, the city said the total amount billed exceeded the $500 million target previously outlined by Gov. Kathy Hochul earlier this year. However, officials did not immediately provide a breakdown showing how the total was calculated across the approximately 7,500 properties. "As Mayor Mamdani has said before, owning a second home worth over 5 million dollars should come with a responsibility to the city that makes it valuable," Julia Agos, a spokesperson for the Department of Finance, said in a statement to Fox News Digital."The Department of Finance will continue to implement the pied-a-terre surcharge fairly and efficiently, ensuring that those most able to contribute do their part to build a city that works for everyone," Agos added. The tax is assessed on a sliding scale based on property values, meaning owners of more expensive homes can face higher charges. JIM GAFFIGAN, NEW YORK LAWMAKERS PUSH GOV HOCHUL TO AXE 'UNNECESSARY TAX' HITTING COMEDY CLUBS In an April report, the New York City comptroller's office estimated that a version of the tax could generate approximately $500 million from more than 11,200 properties before accounting for exemptions and changes in homeowner behavior. After accounting for those factors, however, the report projected that revenue could fall to between roughly $340 million and $380 million. Still, Mamdani has continued to express confidence in the surcharge's revenue potential, telling reporters last week, "We continue to be confident in its ability to raise half a billion dollars per year." The surcharge, approved by the New York state Legislature in May, applies to qualifying luxury second homes in New York City, including certain one- to three-family properties valued at $5 million or more and condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more. MAMDANI WARNING TO WEALTHY NEW YORKERS ABOUT 'FAIR SHARE' SPARKS ONLINE FIRESTORM: 'FULL BLOWN COMMUNIST' Property owners who qualify for exemptions are not subject to the surcharge. Tuesday's announcement comes after a state appeals court handed Mamdani a legal victory earlier this month, unanimously dismissing a lawsuit challenging the rollout of the surcharge. The court found that the homeowners who brought the lawsuit lacked legal standing, overturning a lower court ruling that had ordered the city to restart implementation. However, the tax continues to face separate legal challenges, including questions about its constitutionality. Fox News Digital has reached out to the mayor's office for comment. articles.title: Congress agrees on civilian plane locator mandate after deadly American Airlines-Black Hawk crash
articles.summary: “When military aircraft fly in the same airspace, they must meet the same standards as everyone else.”
articles.body:
(AP) — Congress has agreed to require airliners and other civilian aircraft to carry systems that help pilots locate nearby aircraft. But lawmakers still have to resolve the provisions that apply to the military.

Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash) announced the agreement Tuesday at a demonstration on the lawn outside the Capitol building. A group representing families of the 67 people killed when an American Airlines flight collided with an Army Black Hawk helicopter near Washington, D.C., on Jan. 29, 2025, organized the event.

“When military aircraft fly in the same airspace, they must meet the same standards as everyone else,” said Cantwell, a Democrat representing Washington state.

Cruz, a Texas Republican, said he believes Congress can pass the bill before the end of the year.

On the night of the collision, the Army helicopter flew without the key ADS-B Out system that broadcasts an aircraft’s location because of security concerns, even though it was only on a training flight.

Any aircraft flying in crowded airspace is already required to carry systems that broadcast its location but isn’t required to carry complementary ADS-B In systems that show pilots where nearby aircraft are flying.

“Pilots can’t avoid what we can’t see,” said Capt. Jason Ambrosi, who leads the Air Line Pilots Association union. He said Congress must require these systems on both military and civilian aircraft because the Federal Aviation Administration hasn’t. “Everyone in shared airspace must be seen. Period.”

The Senate and House each passed competing aviation safety reform bills, and lawmakers have been working since the spring to craft a compromise bill addressing 50 recommendations from the National Transportation Safety Board .

Everyone aboard the American Airlines jet, flying from Wichita, Kansas, and the helicopter died when the two aircraft collided. It was the deadliest plane crash on U.S. soil since 2001, and the victims included 28 members of the figure skating community .

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford assured the victims’ families that safety remains the agency’s top priority. The FAA has been in the spotlight since grounding all flights nationwide on Friday because of a technical problem.

The FAA has already taken some steps to prevent helicopters and planes from sharing the same airspace around Reagan airport. Air traffic controllers are now prohibited from relying solely on pilots to see and avoid other aircraft. But the victims’ families and NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy have been pressing for the locator systems.

articles.title: Democrat Mary Peltola flips Alaska Senate seat, defeating GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan
articles.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola defeated Republican Sen.
articles.body: Democrat Mary Peltola defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, NBC News projects, pushing her party’s Senate majority to 56 seats after a stunning wave election. Her party ultimately flipped nine seats in this year’s midterm elections, all but one in states President Donald Trump carried in 2024. Peltola, a former House member, had previously been elected statewide twice before losing her seat two years ago. Now, her Senate victory bolsters a Democratic caucus that will also include members from the likes of Kansas, Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas, forming the largest Senate majority either party has had in 16 years. In a statement Tuesday night, Peltola said she will fight for Alaskans in the Senate. “From Juneau to Utqiagvik, the message from Alaskans is clear: the status quo in DC is not working for Alaska,” Peltola said. “As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.” “As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska’s working families,” she said. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., celebrated Peltola’s projected victory and the wider margin it brings. “With 56 seats, Democrats are in a prime position to create a durable majority that can create lasting, real results for the American people,” he wrote on X. “We must earn back trust by passing bills that lower costs and improve lives — and dare Donald Trump to veto them at his own peril. We will be relentless. This is just the beginning.” Democrats’ 56-seat Senate total will include two independents who caucus with the party: Sens. Angus King of Maine and Bernie Sanders of Vermont. Peltola’s win comes after the Alaska race was roiled in the final days by investigations into allegations of ballot stacking, with a legal battle over a potential spoiler candidate intensifying ahead of Election Day. NBC News reported in July that state and federal prosecutors were investigating the candidacy of Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher and political newcomer who Republicans suspected had been recruited by Democrats to siphon votes from the incumbent, listed as Dan S. Sullivan on Alaska’s ranked choice ballot. Alaska utilizes a voting system in which the top four candidates from the all-party primary advance to the general election. Voters then rank the candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives an initial majority, the fourth-place finisher will be eliminated, and that candidate’s supporters will have their second-choice votes counted. If none of the remaining candidates has more than 50% after that, the same process will repeat for the third-place finisher. Since Peltola won a majority on the first ballot, the race did not go to ranked choice tabulation, which means any confusion over the two Sullivans did not affect the result. A spokesperson for Sen. Sullivan’s campaign said in a statement Monday that Alaskans “deserve a complete and accurate count, and we will let that process run its course until every legal vote is counted and certified.” “We will not be commenting on individual ballot updates or outside projections in the meantime,” campaign spokesperson Nate Adams said. “The campaign will have more to say by the end of this week.” In October, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit aimed at blocking Alaska from certifying the results if the GOP senator lost, a move that Trump told reporters he had ordered. Several days later, The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting the other Sullivan to run. Peltola has denied involvement in Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign, and he has also said it was his own decision to run. In the wake of the report, Trump called for Peltola to be prosecuted, and the Justice Department said it would redouble its efforts to investigate whether any federal laws were broken. The weekend before Election Day, a federal judge dismissed the Trump administration’s effort to segregate ballots cast for Dan J. Sullivan. GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy also ordered a state investigation into Peltola’s campaign. Alaska has not voted for a Democrat for president since 1964, before both Sullivan, 61, and Peltola, 53, were born, and its other Senate seat has been held by a member of the Republican Murkowski dynasty since 1981. But Peltola had won statewide before, having taken Alaska’s at-large House seat in a special election in 2022 and winning one full term that same year. She lapped Sullivan in direct fundraising — $37 million to $14 million through mid-October — which was a constant reminder throughout each quarterly reporting period that she was a formidable challenger. Peltola ran the same playbook as Democrats across the country, yoking Sen. Sullivan to Trump. Though Trump won Alaska three times by double-digit margins, he never reached 55% of the vote. And his second-term policies proved as unpopular in the Last Frontier State as they did with voters in the Lower 48, giving Peltola plenty of room to hammer Sullivan on overall inflation, the Iran war and fuel costs. “Dan’s part of a rigged system where politicians get wealthy and you get hurt,” she said in one ad. “They make cash while our diesel prices go up, our healthcare prices keep rising, and we have fewer fish in our rivers.” Sullivan portrayed Peltola as a tool of Washington Democrats and as a lawmaker in name only. If she made a campaign commercial listing her accomplishments, he said, “that would be the shortest ad in American history.” None of her bills became law, and only one, which would have created a food-security office in the Department of Veterans Affairs, passed in the House. Trump’s efforts to bolster Sullivan included a mid-October campaign visit. But the national wind blew straight across the country to Alaska, and Peltola emerged victorious.

articles.title: Mary Peltola flips Republican Senate seat in Alaska
articles.summary: Former Rep. Mary Peltola, a Democrat, is projected to win the race for Senate in Alaska, defeating GOP incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan and flipping a seat for the Democratic Party, according to Decision Desk HQ. With 94 percent reporting according to DDHQ, Peltola has 50.12 percent of the vote to Sullivan’s 45.79 percent, which puts…
articles.body:
Former Rep. Mary Peltola, a Democrat, is projected to win the race for Senate in Alaska, defeating GOP incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan and flipping a seat for the Democratic Party, according to Decision Desk HQ .

With 94 percent reporting according to DDHQ, Peltola has 50.12 percent of the vote to Sullivan’s 45.79 percent, which puts her above the 50 percent threshold to avoid ranked-choice voting coming into play.

Her win is an upset in a state that generally leans Republican, signaling that support for President Trump dragged down incumbent Republicans this year.

The race had been very competitive all summer, in part due to Peltola’s unique profile as a candidate, Sullivan’s ties to the unpopular war in Iran and President Trump and the independent nature of Alaska politics .

Peltola also tried to hit Sullivan over his ties to large trawling companies headquartered in Washington and Oregon and link the practice of large-scale trawling to the diminishing fish stocks in Alaska.

Peltola, 53, is a two-term former congresswoman who has also worked on fishing boats and campaigns and has served in local government and as a tribal judge. She was raised in the Kuskokwim River region in southwest Alaska and now lives in Anchorage.

Peltola will become the first Alaska Native senator. While a congresswoman, she stood out from many in her caucus for supporting the oil and gas industry and gun ownership. She introduced bipartisan legislation to limit trawling, a type of commercial fishing, and pressed the need for institutional reform in Congress like term limits and stock trading bans.

In the House, she was a leader of the Blue Dog Caucus, a group of moderate Democrats that also included Reps. Jared Golden (D-Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.).

During the Senate campaign, the Sullivan campaign and national Republican groups ran attacks targeting Peltola’s treatment of her staff based on a New York Times report in which former aides alleged Peltola demeaned and berated staff. Republicans also hit Peltola over votes she took in Congress, including against a version of an annual defense bill.

The race could put Alaska in the crosshairs of federal intervention. The Department of Justice sued in October to block the results if Sullivan lost, arguing that an independent candidate by the same name, Dan Sullivan, would lead to voter confusion.

articles.title: Alaska Dem Peltola defeats Sullivan, flipping 9th GOP Senate seat after 'decoy Dan' uproar
articles.summary: Democrats seized a 56-44 majority in the U.S. Senate after Mary Peltola defeated Alaska Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in a race that featured a same-name ballot challenger.
articles.body: Democrats flipped a ninth GOP-held Senate seat in the 2026 midterm elections, with former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola defeating two-term Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in a state that President Donald Trump carried in 2024. Peltola's victory gives Democrats a 56-44 majority in the U.S. Senate. The contest emerged as one of the nation's most closely watched Senate races, with Republicans defending a seat in a state President Donald Trump carried by roughly 13 percentage points in 2024, and Democrats eyeing a rare opportunity to make inroads in traditionally Republican territory. The controversy deepened just days before Election Day when The New York Times reported that Peltola campaign aides, attorneys and national Democratic operatives had participated in a secret effort to recruit a candidate sharing the Republican incumbent's name. According to the Times, text messages and interviews revealed a broader operation, internally dubbed the "ballot composition project," aimed at recruiting candidates who could siphon votes from Sullivan. The effort reportedly involved the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and included discussions about establishing a new right-wing political party. Peltola's campaign denied involvement with either Sullivan campaign, while the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) also rejected allegations of participation. The revelations prompted Republican Gov. Michael Dunleavy to order an investigation into whether the alleged recruitment effort violated Alaska law. The Cook Political Report rated the contest a toss-up, reflecting the unusually competitive environment in a state that has generally favored Republicans in federal elections. Peltola, a former state lawmaker, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election to succeed the late Republican Rep. Don Young. GOP SENATOR, EX-HOUSE DEM EMERGE FROM ALASKA’S ‘JUNGLE PRIMARY’ DESPITE FAR-LEFT MEDDLING She defeated former Republican Gov. Sarah Palin in that contest before winning a full term later that year. Peltola subsequently lost her 2024 reelection bid to Republican Nick Begich III, setting the stage for her Senate campaign. Sullivan, a Marine Corps veteran and former Alaska attorney general, first won his Senate seat in 2014 by defeating Democratic incumbent Mark Begich, Nick's uncle. He secured reelection in 2020 and sought a third term emphasizing his experience, national security and Alaska's energy interests. The 2026 race also featured an unusual ballot controversy involving Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher who shared nearly the same name as the Republican incumbent. Alaska election officials initially moved to remove the second Sullivan from the ballot amid allegations that his candidacy was intended to confuse voters or siphon support from the senator. The candidate denied wrongdoing, and the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that he could remain on the ballot. The DOJ sued in October to mitigate any "misleading" impact of the newcomer Sullivan. COURT KEEPS ‘DECOY DAN’ ON ALASKA BALLOT AS EXPERT WARNS RANKED-CHOICE SYSTEM CREATES VOTER ‘TRAPS’ The controversy added another complication to Alaska's ranked-choice voting system, which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference. Under the system, a candidate receiving a majority of first-choice votes wins outright. Otherwise, the lowest-performing candidate is eliminated, and ballots are redistributed according to voters' next available preferences until a winner emerges. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Peltola had previously benefited from the system during her 2022 congressional victories, when ranked-choice tabulation helped determine the outcomes of races featuring multiple Republican opponents. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Alaska contest carried national significance as both parties battled over control of the Senate, with the result determining whether Republicans retained the seat or Democrats added it to their column.

articles.title: Mary Peltola flips Alaska Senate seat in another Democratic win
articles.summary: The hard-fought contest is the last to be called for the US Senate and likely faces legal challenges.
articles.body:
Democrat Mary Peltola has defeated incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan in the race for Alaska’s Senate seat, delivering a final blow to Republicans in a midterm election rout following a race that drew accusations of cheating.

The Associated Press (AP) news agency called the race on Tuesday night, capping a contest that attracted national attention after an investigation alleged that aides to Peltola recruited another man named Dan Sullivan to run for office to siphon votes from the Republican incumbent.

Peltola has denied any knowledge of the alleged decoy candidate plot.

Sullivan had pledged to accept the election outcome days after the Department of Justice filed a lawsuit seeking to decertify the results if the Republican incumbent lost.

Peltola, in a statement on social media, said there “is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs and put Alaska first. Thank you, Alaska. Let’s get to work.”

Alaska also elected a Democrat as governor for the first time since 1998, after former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republicans, including one endorsed by US President Donald Trump. AP has not yet called the US House race, where independent candidate Bill Hill is challenging Republican Representative Nick Begich.

The Alaska race is the last US Senate contest to be resolved in this year’s midterm elections, and Peltola’s victory expands the Democrats’ majority after they retook control of the chamber. The party already won campaigns in conservative states including South Carolina, Texas, Kansas and, most recently, Mississippi.

With Peltola’s victory, Democrats flipped nine Senate seats, the most since 1958. Republicans entered the midterms with a 53-47 majority, while Democrats now emerge with a 56-44 margin.

Peltola previously held the state’s lone House seat, making her the first Alaska Native to serve in Congress. She lost her bid for a second full term to Begich in 2024, but she became central to Democrats’ plans to retake the Senate in 2026.

During the campaign, Peltola tapped into Alaskans’ frustrations with high fuel prices and other costs. Those concerns hit especially hard in remote communities that rely on diesel for electricity and heat and are often only accessible by air or water.

Her campaign peppered social media with photos of her travels around the state as she sought to distance herself from national Democrats and build a coalition around a platform of “Alaska first”.

“Alaskans who know me know that I’m not liberal or radical,” Peltola said. “I am only interested in working for Alaska and working for the best interest of Alaskans, in as nonpartisan of a way as I possibly can.”

The race attracted a flood of spending by outside groups and at times turned negative, with the campaigns accusing each other of spreading lies. Trump and Vice President JD Vance made separate trips to the state in the month before the election in support of the incumbent.
