articles.title: Democrat Mary Peltola unseats Republican in Alaska Senate race
articles.summary: Confirmation of Mary Peltola's victory caps of the party's rout of the Republicans in the midterms Senate election.
articles.body:
Democrat Mary Peltola has won Alaska's hard-fought Senate race, completing a sweeping victory for the party in the US upper house in the midterm elections.

The win gives the Democrats a 56th Senate seat following a tumultuous and controversial election in Alaska, which featured alleged spoiler recruitment efforts and unprecedented court battles.

It took two full weeks of counting to call a winner in the 3 November poll due to the logistical challenge of collecting ballots from across the state's remote expanse.

The Democratic win is the ninth Senate seat the party took from Republicans in this year's midterms, giving the party control of the US Congress for the last two years of Donald Trump's presidency.

A historic set of victories nationally also saw the party win back the House of Representatives.

In her victory statement, Peltola said the "status quo in DC is not working for Alaska".

She recalled speaking to "elders in tears about empty fish racks" and to parents in rural Alaska choosing between heating their homes and putting food on the table.

Peltola's campaign had come under fire after the New York Times reported Democrats attempted to recruit a candidate named Daniel J Sullivan, a complete political unknown residing in a small coastal town who shared a name with the state's current US Senator and incumbent, Dan S Sullivan, in an alleged attempt to confuse voters.

Trump says Alaska voters chose the wrong Dan Sullivan. What does the data show?

Could Alaska's fishing industry tilt Washington's balance of power?

After legal challenges, state courts ruled the second Daniel J Sullivan could remain on the ballot, and election officials distinguished them on election materials.

Peltola denied having knowledge of the alleged plot but her campaign swiftly came under fire, and both the justice department and Alaska's Republican governor said they would launch investigations.

The Trump administration then filed a lawsuit attempting to stop the certification of the election results if the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan lost.

A federal judge, though, dismissed the case, following legal challenges from Alaska election officials as well as the Peltola campaign and voting groups.

Due to Alaska's ranked-choice voting system, voters confused about which Dan Sullivan was the incumbent could simply choose each man as their first and second choice.

If they did so, after the first round of voting was complete, tabulation would re-allocate any votes from the non-incumbent Dan Sullivan - who stood little to no chance of winning - to the US Senator.

Experts told the BBC that this process made it difficult for any potential spoiler candidate to have any impact on the results.

An analysis by BBC Verify found that even if every vote for the other Dan Sullivan had gone to the incumbent, Peltola would still have won.

The seat initially was one of several toss-up races that appeared as a must-win for Democrats if they wanted to gain control of the Senate - but by the time Peltola was called the winner, they had seats to spare.

With 99% of ballots counted, Peltola had slightly more than 50%, while Sullivan trailed on less than 46%.

Sullivan, a former Alaska attorney general and an ally of Trump, campaigned on his record of delivering energy and military investment for the state.

Peltola promised Alaskans a more independent voice in Washington.

"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," she said in her victory statement.

"I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families."

articles.title: Video shows ICE agent pepper spraying pregnant U.S. citizen
articles.summary: Video circulating on social media shows ICE officers throwing a 23-year-old woman, Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, to the ground during a detainment outside of the jail.
articles.body:
( KTXL ) – A pregnant California woman was sent to the hospital after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers allegedly pushed her during a protest outside a Stanislaus County jail in Modesto, the woman’s family said.

Video circulating on social media shows ICE officers throwing a 23-year-old woman, Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, to the ground during a detainment outside of the jail.

Andrade is a U.S. citizen, Patrick Kolasiński, the lawyer representing her and her husband, said in a Monday news release.

Andrade, her husband, and sister-in-law, were outside the jail to protest “ICE agents detaining people as they are released from county custody,” her legal representation explained.

In one video, three officers appear to pull Andrade — whom her lawyer said is 12 weeks pregnant — to the ground after she appears to place her hands on one officer. Andrade’s lawyer said she was also pepper-sprayed during the incident.

Andrade was held for several hours by ICE before she was released, according to her legal representation.

“The agents’ conduct raises serious questions about the justification for Monica’s initial detention, the force used against a pregnant woman, and the treatment of American citizens during federal immigration operations,” Andrade’s lawyer said in a statement. “It also raises broader questions about what is happening at the Stanislaus County Jail and the role of local law enforcement.”

The Modesto Police Department wrote in a social media post Monday that they are “aware of recent federal immigration enforcement activity” and that it did not conduct or assist in the detainment, following California law.

A spokesperson for the Stanislaus County Sheriff’s Office similarly told Nexstar’s KTXL that they are aware of the incident involving Andrade and that its deputies do not assist in federal enforcement operations.

Video shared by the woman’s family shows Andrade being carried out on a stretcher to a Stockton-area hospital following the detention. One person who appears to be an ICE officer is seen exiting the ambulance alongside Andrade.

Following a medical evaluation, Andrade and her unborn child are “doing well,” her lawyer said.

The Modesto incident follows a recent surge in federal immigration enforcement activity across Northern California and the Bay Area, drawing scrutiny from community members and lawmakers. On Sept. 16, ICE officers arrested Ann Lawani, a nurse and professor from Lodi , in what the U.S. Department of Homeland Security called a “targeted enforcement operation.”

Andrade is at home with her family, her lawyer said.

As of Tuesday afternoon, the Department of Homeland Security has not commented on the incident.

articles.title: Huang agrees to testify before Senate Banking panel
articles.summary: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, a spokesperson for Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) confirmed Tuesday. Lawmakers have ramped up scrutiny of Huang’s alleged extramarital affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, who worked as an executive at computing company Megaspeed, over concerns that China may have gained…
articles.body:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, a spokesperson for Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) confirmed Tuesday.

Lawmakers have ramped up scrutiny of Huang’s alleged extramarital affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, who worked as an executive at computing company Megaspeed, over concerns that China may have gained access to advanced AI chips and other sensitive technology.

Scott formally requested Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick appear before the panel at separate hearings, warning that the former Nvidia chief could be subpoenaed if he refused to appear voluntarily.

In his letter to Huang sent last week, Scott sought a Dec. 3 hearing in the wake of the affair scandal that raised national security questions about whether Chinese-based companies were able to obtain U.S. semiconductor technology through the relationship.

Huang has also agreed to testify at a closed-door hearing before three House committees, who have been conducting their own investigation into the matter. His appearance before the Senate Banking Committee would mark his first public testimony before Congress.

The developments add to a tumultuous week for Huang, who resigned Thursday after news broke that he engaged in extramarital affairs, including a second alleged affair with an employee.

Huang admitted that he was “unfaithful” to his wife of 41 years and seemingly confirmed the relationship with Alice Huang, who shares his last name but is not related. Singapore-based company Megaspeed, where Alice Huang worked as an executive, is a customer of Nvidia.

Nvidia’s board launched an investigation into the incident and Huang swiftly resigned from the AI chip giant. President Trump, Tesla CEO Elon Musk and other prominent figures called on the board to reinstate Huang, whose chips are crucial for powering development.

Trump called Huang an “honorable guy” and said he was not aware that the Megaspeed executive was an operative for China.

Huang on Tuesday said he would be “honored” to return to his role at the company he co-founded should he get the board’s approval, telling The Hill he received an “outpouring of calls” from some Nvidia staff, investors, business partners and customers for him to return as CEO.

But the board on Tuesday rejected Huang’s offer to return as CEO, closing the door on his immediate reinstatement despite pressure from Silicon Valley and public support from Trump and other administration officials.

Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said the board had “unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is currently serving as the interim head of the company while its board searches for a permanent successor.

articles.title: Ignatius Farray, cómico, responde a Ayuso: "Está tan gastado decir que la culpa es de los inmigrantes, que ahora es de los andaluces"
articles.standfirst: Ignatius Farray contesta al discurso de Ayuso sobre Andalucía con una dura crítica social
articles.summary: Ignatius Farray contesta al discurso de Ayuso sobre Andalucía con una dura crítica social
articles.body: El debate político y cultural en España ha vuelto a encenderse tras un reciente cruce de declaraciones entre la presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, y el humorista Ignatius Farray. La controversia gira en torno a la gestión pública, los flujos migratorios internos y el uso de los territorios como argumento en la contienda partidista, generando una oleada de reacciones en redes sociales y medios de comunicación. El origen de la polémica se sitúa en una intervención de la dirigente madrileña sobre el modelo de gestión histórica del sur de España y su relación con los ciudadanos que residen en la capital. En su discurso, Ayuso manifestó textualmente: "¿Qué es la estrategia de la carcoma? Poquito a poco, va cayendo todo. La decadencia es tóxica y se pega en todas partes, y después nos encontramos como la Andalucía socialista, que durante 40 años gracias a esa red de gente garrapatera que vivía del dinero de todos, resulta que Andalucía, muchos de aquí sois andaluces y por eso estáis viviendo en la Comunidad de Madrid". Lejos de suavizar el tono, la líder autonómica enumeró una serie de problemas estructurales para defender su postura frente a la gestión de la izquierda. Ante el público presente, Ayuso prosiguió con su argumentario asegurando: "Fracaso escolar, abandono escolar, corrupción, Andalucía la última siempre en puestos de trabajo, en desastres, siempre de los centros de salud cerrados todas las tardes en verano porque estaban de vacaciones. La decadencia llama a la decadencia, que no nos acostumbremos a la decadencia, porque si te acostumbras a la decadencia te van a pisar todo en la vida". Estas palabras provocaron una inmediata contestación desde el ámbito de la comedia, que suele funcionar como termómetro crítico de la actualidad institucional. Con su habitual estilo irreverente y de sátira social, el humorista tinerfeño decidió intervenir para cuestionar los argumentos empleados por la presidenta regional y señalar un supuesto desplazamiento en el foco de los culpables habituales del discurso político. Para zanjar la cuestión con su característica ironía, Ignatius Farray resumió su postura sobre el mensaje de la dirigente popular sentenciando sin filtros: "Está tan gastado ya decir que la culpa es de los inmigrantes, que ahora dicen que la culpa es de los andaluces".
